vessels.name: Dugout canoe
rows: Sugime, 7.6 m cedar: Taiwan→Yonaguni, 225 km in 45 h ≈ 2.5–3 kn
the paddle itself — nothing is hung on the hull
vessels.text:
No watercraft survives from the crossing to Sahul. That people arrived is certain; what they arrived in is not, and this model does not draw the vessel.

What the record does support is a negative: **bamboo rafts do not work.** Kaifu's experimental crossings (National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo, 2016–19) found rafts made under a knot against the 1–2 knot Kuroshio and failed outright, while a 7.6 m cedar dugout crossed 225 km of open water in 45 hours. If the Pleistocene sea craft was anything, it was more like a dugout than a raft.

The date is itself contested: Madjedbebe's optically stimulated luminescence gives 65 ± 6 ka (Clarkson et al., *Nature*, 2017); Allen and O'Connell argue for ~50 ka.
vessels.cite: Clarkson et al. 2017; Kealy, Louys & O'Connor 2018; Kaifu experimental crossings 2016–19.

polar.rigNote: Paddled. The one measured figure is a crossing, not a sprint: a 7.6 m cedar dugout took 225 km of the Kuroshio, Taiwan to Yonaguni, in 45 hours — very close to 3 kn held for two days, and that is the paddling floor the router holds in any wind, including a calm. The rise off the wind is the fair-wind mat sail of the Pacific logboats (Haddon & Hornell), set only when the wind serves; no mast is drawn, and none is attested this early.
polar.rig: paddles, with a mat sail for fair winds

anchor.source: Kaifu's Sugime crossing 2019: 225 km in 45 h ≈ 3 kn; Haddon & Hornell, Canoes of Oceania, for the fair-wind sail

floor.source: Kaifu's Sugime crossing for the floor. No measured logboat headwind figure exists; the loss is Olympias's fractional windage (46% of floor at 8 m/s) carried over — an inference, stated as one

hull.steeringProvenance: Steering is ATTESTED as a negative: the one measured performance row is a paddled crossing (Kaifu’s Sugime, Taiwan→Yonaguni, 2019), the polar’s own note reads “Paddled”, and nothing hung on the hull is attested anywhere this early. The paddle is crew gear, no crew is drawn, so the hull mounts nothing.

vessels.name: Voyaging canoe
rows: 18.7 m LOA · 4.72 m beam · 0.76 m draught
**two masts**, crab claw — a triangular sail on two spars along its long sides
a long paddle, not a rudder
Hawaiʻi→Tahiti 1976, ~2,400 nm in 30 days at sea ≈ 3.3 kn
lashed-lug planking, no metal at all
vessels.text:
A double-hulled sailing canoe: two hulls of equal length lashed side by side, carrying two masts and steered by a long paddle rather than a rudder. Austronesian voyagers using vessels of this kind settled the Pacific islands, reaching the Lapita range by about 900 BC and Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa later.

The crab claw is approximately an isosceles triangle carried on two light spars along its long sides. It generates lift rather than merely catching wind, and it **widens upwards**, putting sail area high where the wind is stronger — which also raises the heeling moment, and is why the rig is carried on a multihull. A double hull carries enough sail to use it, and the combination makes good about 75° to the true wind, against roughly 90° for a square rig in ordinary conditions.

Lashed-lug construction uses planks carved with integral internal lugs and lashed to ribs with fibre — no nails, no iron, nothing that corrodes.
vessels.cite: Irwin, *Archaeology in Oceania* 58 (2023); Finney, *Science* (1977); Polynesian Voyaging Society logs.

polar.rigNote: Poor by modern standards, positive by ancient ones — and positive is the whole argument, because it is what lets a canoe beat back the way she came. Fastest on a broad reach, not before the wind.
polar.rig: crab claw on a double hull

anchor.source: Finney, Hōkūleʻa Hawaiʻi→Tahiti 1976: ~100 nm/day, best days near 7 kn

hull.steeringProvenance: ATTESTED by her own card row — “Steering: a long paddle, not a rudder” (Hōkūleʻa; Finney 1977, Polynesian Voyaging Society logs). The steering sweep is handled by the steersman over the quarter, not hung on the hull; no crew is drawn, so nothing is mounted. Before round 121 the model hung a pintled stern rudder on EACH hull.

vessels.name: Trireme
rows: Beam of the HULL, at the waterline
9.7 — as slender as a modern frigate
~5.4 kn; 2.9 kn into a headwind and 1 m sea
about 200 — 170 rowers (62 thranitai, 54 zygitai, 54 thalamitai), ~14 deck crew, 10–20 marines
180° in one minute, inside 2.5 ship-lengths — measured on Olympias
two masts, both square: the main and a small foremast, struck before battle
two pēdalia, one over each quarter — the pair Olympias steers with

none is drawn, because her navy's own record answers — the Athenian dockyard inventories list each warship's entire gear down to her two iron anchors, weighed on the stone at under half a hundredweight, and eight cables, four for the bow anchors and four to moor her stern to the shore; no winding machine is among the equipment. The machines of her era stood ashore: Herodotus watched the Hellespont bridge cables tautened from the land with wooden windlasses in this hull's own year, and Delos charged ships dues for the use of the harbour windlass. Two hundred hands worked her light anchors by direct pull (inference)
vessels.text:
A hull built to carry a bronze ram at speed and to turn inside its own length. It is also the best-measured ancient ship in existence, because one was built.

*Olympias* (1987) **fell short of what the ancient sources imply**, and the shortfall is the interesting part. Xenophon implies 7–8 knots sustained for sixteen hours; the reconstruction managed 8.3 knots for a sprint and about 5.4 sustained. Coates concluded the hull is roughly 10% overweight and too short — Vitruvius's two-cubit oar spacing at the longer Ionic cubit gives a hull over 40 m, and a Mark II on those lines was calculated to reach 9.7 kn sprint and 7.5 sustained. It has never been built.

The widely repeated 8.9 knots was a single momentary GPS reading; the Final Report says 8.3 kn is the honest figure, 'achieved only momentarily (if at all)'.
vessels.cite: Rankov (ed.), *Trireme Olympias: The Final Report* (Oxbow, 2012); Morrison, Coates & Rankov, *The Athenian Trireme*.

polar.rigNote: A galley goes where it likes and not far, and the figure above is her SAILING speed — the sail is for fair winds only. Under oar: 8.3 kn sprint, 5.4 kn cruise, and about 2.9 kn into a headwind with a metre of sea — measured on the reconstruction Olympias, which fell short of what the ancient sources imply and is thought to be ~10% too short in the hull. The router holds the 5.4 as her oar floor in any wind, falling to the measured 2.9 dead upwind in a fresh breeze.
polar.rig: oars, with a square sail for fair winds

anchor.source: Olympias Final Report: 8.3 kn "achieved only momentarily", cruise 5.4 under oar

floor.source: Olympias sea trials: 5.4 kn oar cruise; ~2.9 kn into a head sea at force 4–5, taken at the polar's 8 m/s reference — (5.4 − 2.9)/8

hull.steeringProvenance: A pair of pēdalia, one over each quarter, is the attested steering of the type: Morrison, Coates & Rankov, The Athenian Trireme, and the reconstruction Olympias, whose helmsman works both looms from one seat. DERIVED here in size: blade and loom are scaled off the hull’s own draught and beam, no ancient steering oar surviving to measure.
hull.windlassProvenance: JUDGED SILENT, r179 — the windlass question for this hull, the last of the r172 line, closes with nothing drawn, and on a third shape of silence: not r176's inference stack over a later-era machine, not r178's tradition with nothing to extend, but a complete inventory that omits the machine. The Athenian navy kept stone-cut inventories of its dockyards — the fullest gear record of any ancient ship class — and the lists of entire equipment (entele skeue) supplied to three- and four-banked ships from 330/329 BC enumerate everything aboard: two iron anchors per warship (CIA II 807/808/809/811, 'ankyras sideras dyo' in every case), eight cables in two recorded sizes, four for the bow anchors and four shore-cables (epigya) that moored her stern to the beach (Torr, Ancient Ships 1894, notes 161 and 166, the inscriptions quoted verbatim), the hypozomata among the hanging gear, oars, rudders, ladders, poles, masts, yards, sails, screens — and no windlass, winch or capstan anywhere. The inventory even weighs the anchors: CIA II 807 col. b (329 BC) records iron anchors at a stated weight of twenty-odd mnas — under half a hundredweight in Torr's reading of the damaged numeral, named as his. Torr's whole book, downloaded in r177 and grepped again this round, has one windlass sentence (p. 95), and it is the sail-tackle of the big Roman merchantmen — the corbita's own r177 evidence. The Greek word for the shipboard machine, stropheion, boards a ship exactly once in the record, on Lucian's Isis (Nav. 5, c. AD 165, the corbita's r177 warrant, six centuries after this hull's drawn year); its classical-era epigraphic use is the Delian harbour accounts (IG XI(2).138 B 8, iv/iii BC; LSJ s.v.), where stropheia are dues ships paid for the USE of a windlass — the machine stood on the quay. And Herodotus' own word for it, onos, appears in this hull's own drawn year: the Hellespont bridge cables of 480 BC, laid over pontoon triremes, were made taut from the land — ek ges — with wooden windlasses, onoisi xylinoisi (Hdt. 7.36.3, fetched verbatim in Greek and English; LSJ's other windlass citations are a bone-setting frame and the Mechanics, none shipboard). Her world knew the machine; its place was the shore, and aboard her it had no work: anchors of under ~25 kg, some 200 hands, a 47 t hull moored stern-to with her own listed shore-cables and hauled out on the ship-sheds' slipways — she was the thing the shore's machines and men hauled. r177 drew the corbita's windlass because her ship's own gear list names one; this hull's own gear lists, far fuller than Lucian's sentence, omit it — the same class of source, obeyed both ways. Stated: the entire-gear lists are the 4th-century navy's, some 150 years after the drawn year (-480); they are the class's fullest record at any date and the 5th-century evidence points the same way, but the gap is named. Scope: the judgment is for the classical trireme as her navy inventoried her; the giant polyremes of the Hellenistic age are different ships, and their gear (Moschion's forty carried twelve anchors) is not read backward here. That the crew worked anchors and hypozomata by direct pull is an inference, marked as one on the card. Named as not fetched: Morrison, Coates & Rankov's The Athenian Trireme and Rankov's Olympias Final Report (both gated; both already this card's cited hull sources), and the IG II2 stones beyond Torr's transcriptions (PHI search script-gated, Attic Inscriptions Online HTTP 500 for IG II2 1604) — any of them, fetched and attesting a shipboard winding machine on a trireme, reopens the question.

vessels.name: Roman merchantman
rows: one mainmast with a broad square mainsail; larger ships carried more than one mast and more than one sail per mast — the raked *artemon* forward and a triangular *supparum* above the main (Casson)
no reef points: brailing lines ran through lead or bone rings sewn to the sail and gathered it up to the yard
55 m; beam over a quarter of that; hold 13 m deep; 1,200–1,300 t of grain (Lucian) — contested, some read 1,900 t
Alexandria→Rome laden a month, sometimes two or more
about 70 days; 2,000–3,000 voyages a year fed the city
a pair of great quarter rudders — the Sidon and Portus reliefs draw them; no Roman ship shows a sternpost rudder
vessels.text:
The bulk carrier of the Roman Mediterranean, built shell-first with pegged mortise-and-tenon joints and double planking. Typical hulls ran 20–30 m and carried 150–350 tons; the standard grain capacity was 50,000 *modii*, about 350 tonnes.

The rig is a single broad square mainsail on one mast, with a small raked *artemon* over the bows on larger ships and sometimes a triangular *supparum* above the main. It was handled by **brailing**: there are no reef points, and the yard does not come down. Lines ran up the face of the sail through rings of lead or bone sewn to the cloth, and hauling on them gathered the sail up to the yard like a curtain.

The same ship on the same route took ten days to a fortnight in one direction and a month or more in the other. The difference is the wind: the Etesian northerlies of the eastern Mediterranean blow steadily down toward Egypt in summer. The grain fleet ran downwind to Alexandria in ballast and beat its way home laden, a round trip of about seventy days, and the sailing season closed in winter when the *mare clausum* held from November to March.
vessels.cite: Casson, *Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World* (1971); Lucian, *The Ship*; Wikipedia, *Grain supply to the city of Rome* and *Square rig* (accessed 2026-08-02).

polar.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

anchor.source: Casson, Ships and Seamanship: Puteoli→Alexandria ~9 d fair; favorable runs 4.5–6 kn

hull.steeringProvenance: Roman seagoing ships steer with a pair of great quarter rudders — the Sidon and Portus reliefs and the Ostia mosaics draw them, and no Roman wreck or image shows a sternpost rudder (Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World). DERIVED in size from the hull; the reliefs are profile carvings with no usable scale.
hull.windlassProvenance: The gear list of her own trade's giant, thirty-five years before her drawn year. Lucian, Navigium 5 (c. AD 165), on the Alexandrian grain freighter Isis at Piraeus — the ship this card's own rows carry: 'αἱ ἄγκυραι καὶ στροφεῖα καὶ περιαγωγεῖς καὶ αἱ κατὰ τὴν πρύμναν οἰκήσεις, θαυμάσια πάντα μοι ἔδοξε' — the anchors, the windlasses and the capstans, and the stern cabins, all of them wonders to the visitor. Torr (Ancient Ships, 1894, p. 95) and the fetched translation read the two nouns as the ship's winding machines; which noun is the horizontal machine the text does not say, and ONLY the horizontal windlass is drawn — a Roman vertical winch has no attested form, and the Georgian capstan this hull carried until r172 was exactly that anachronism, removed. Lucretius 4.901–906 puts the machina with its trocleae and tympana — pulleys and drums moving great weights at light effort — in the same breath as the ship and her rudder; Torr's note connects the Latin terms to Lucian's Greek ones, a scholarly reading named as such. Warrant: GEAR-LIST EXTENSION, same trade, same era — one stated inference, from the 55 m Isis down the same Alexandria–Rome run to the drawn 40 m carrier (the Madrague de Giens size, the card's other named wreck). Station u 0.15 is a PLACEMENT INFERENCE ±0.05: no ancient source places the machine; the bower anchors and their cables work at the bow — hawse-eyes and catheads a little abaft them (Torr pp. 69–74) — and the drawn station is the open foredeck abaft the artemon's step. Barrel 3.6 m is a GEOMETRIC read off the drawn deck's breadth at that station (probe, read-only, before this record was written); diameter 0.5 m, the axis a foot over the deck and the two standards are Falconer CLASS DEFAULTS cross-tradition (r173). CONTESTED, the standing negative: Laurons 2, the one wreck preserved to the rail (late 3rd c. AD, a ~15 m, ~30 t coaster), keeps her bitts, belaying pins and spare rudder and shows NO windlass in any fetched description — the class's small end may have worked its anchors by hand, and a corbita drawn at her size would reopen this judgment toward silence. No fetched relief or mosaic shows the machine; Casson 1971 is borrow-gated and was not readable this round, named as such.

vessels.name: Sewn-plank dhow
rows: one to three masts carrying **settee** sails — a quadrilateral, a lateen with its forward point cut off — sometimes a true lateen
*baghlah* the heavy deep-sea trader · *boum* large, tapering stern · *sambuk* the largest still sailing in the Gulf · *jalibut* small to medium
about 30 on a large dhow, about 12 on a small one
coir stitching through drilled holes; no iron
out on the SW monsoon Apr–Sep, home on the NE Nov–Mar
twin lashed quarter rudders, as the Belitung hull is reconstructed — a sewn ship has no iron to hang a pintle on

her own wreck's anchor — a composite grapnel, four wrought-iron arms crossing at two levels round a bell-shaped cast-iron weight, on a hardwood shank; the arms 1.7 m across, read off the excavation drawing's own scale bar; stowed loose on deck at the bow, the tradition's stow, a coir cable bent to the shank head. The shank's full length did not survive and is drawn at a stated reconstruction (inference)

none is drawn, because none is attested — not on her own wreck, whose only nautical equipment is the composite grapnel (wooden shank, iron arms); not anywhere in the tradition's 7th–16th-century survey, which describes the anchors of every period and no winding machine; and not at its documented end, where Gulf craft stow the anchor loose on deck or hang it on the kalba beam at the prow, and the winch arrives with the engine. Her grapnel worked by the crew's direct pull — twelve to thirty hands — is the read backward from that practice (inference)
vessels.text:
A sewn-plank trader of one to three masts. The sail is usually a **settee** rather than a true lateen: a quadrilateral, in effect a lateen with its forward point cut off, so the luff is short and the yard still rakes steeply.

In the Indian Ocean the departure **date** is not a free variable. The monsoon reverses twice a year, and it is the only wind system on Earth that does, so the calendar of the whole ocean is fixed by it: Egypt to India leaving in July on the south-west monsoon, home from November on the north-east.

The *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* states the month outright — 'about the month of July, that is Epiphi' — four separate times, for four separate routes.

Sewn construction with no iron at all was not primitive. It flexed on a reef instead of splitting, and it could be repaired anywhere there was coir.
vessels.cite: *Periplus Maris Erythraei* §§14, 24, 39, 49, 56; Flecker on the Belitung wreck.

polar.rigNote: Better than a square rig, and by less than the textbooks claim — their 55–65° is a heading. The cost is manpower: tacking means walking the whole yard round the mast.

anchor.source: Villiers, Sons of Sindbad: monsoon day's runs ~130 nm

hull.steeringProvenance: Her own construction row — coir stitching, no iron — refuses the pintle-and-gudgeon fitting the model hung before round 121: a pintle is an iron hinge. The Belitung hull (this card’s own row, c. AD 830) is reconstructed with twin lashed quarter rudders (Jewel of Muscat, 2010). The stern-hung rudder belongs to the ocean’s later big types — baghlah, ghanjah — whose rows here are burden figures, not fittings; the drawn ship is the sewn early type.
hull.grapnelProvenance: DRAWN, r182 — the head of the anchors line, on the strongest warrant any ground tackle in this fleet carries: the drawn instance's own wreck preserved the anchor. Flecker's excavation report names it — 'the ship's nautical equipment may be represented by a composite grapnel-type anchor, the shank of wood and the arms of iron' (World Archaeology 32:3, 2001; the hedge is the author's) — and the excavation monograph gives the form: the arms protrude straight outward and are separated vertically by a heavy bell-shaped iron disk with a hole through the centre, the disk a shape that lends itself to casting, the arms thought to be wrought iron; only the lower end of the wooden shank survived, and one arm is broken (Flecker in Krahl, Guy, Wilson & Raby, Shipwrecked: Tang Treasures and Monsoon Winds, Smithsonian 2010, pp. 112–13, figs. 84–85, fetched whole this round). DIMENSIONS are the plate's own: fig. 84 carries a 100 cm scale bar, read at 2.5 px/cm in a 300-dpi render — the intact arm pair 1.72 m tip to tip (plan and both elevations agree within 4 mm of drawing), the crossing pair 1.44 m as drawn with its broken arm, arm shafts ~0.12 m as drawn (concretion not separable; the model draws 0.10 m), the bell ~0.55 m across the base and ~0.13 m high, the shank stub ~0.16–0.20 m thick, its foot protruding below the bell. The broken pair is drawn complete at the intact pair's span (inference). The SHANK'S LENGTH is preserved nowhere: 1.8 m is a reconstruction — about the arm span over again, shank enough for the crown to trip and the head to take the cable clear of the arms — and no fetched source preserves or reconstructs it. Shank timber Afzelia sp. or Amoora sp. (CSIRO identification, Flecker 2001); the bell may be Chinese-cast — cast iron was China's alone in the 9th century — and the tradition's own navigational literature names an iron grapnel al-hadid, 'the iron', and an anchor type al-anjar al-siniya, 'the Chinese anchor' (Ibn Majid, via Flecker 2010). STOW: loose on deck at the bow — the tradition's documented practice at its recorded end (Lockerbie, catnaps.org, r178's fetch: Gulf craft stow the anchor loose on deck or hang it on the kalba at the prow), and the Maqamat images hang the four-pronged grapnel at the prow (Agius, Classic Ships of Islam, 2008, ill. 32, form only, no scale readable). That a 9th-century crew stowed it the same way is an inference between those attestations; station u 0.125 — the open foredeck between the stem and the foremast's step — and the stow attitude (the shank laid aft and yawed to pass the mast's foot, measured against the drawn deck) are PLACEMENT INFERENCE: no source places the anchor aboard. Named as not fetched: the Jewel of Muscat replica's build record (jewelofmuscat.tv unreachable this round, HTTP 404 on every tried path) and Vosmer's PSAS paper (pay-gated, r178) — either, fetched and giving a reconstructed shank, would replace the stated 1.8 m.
hull.windlassProvenance: JUDGED SILENT, r178 — the windlass question for this hull, opened by the r172 residual, closes with nothing drawn, and this field says why. The drawn ship is the sewn early type (this record's own steering provenance), the Belitung wreck's tradition, and the evidence is silent at every documented point of that tradition. Her own wreck's excavation report, read whole this round, mentions no windlass, winch or capstan anywhere; the ship's nautical equipment 'may be represented by a composite grapnel-type anchor, the shank of wood and the arms of iron' (Flecker, World Archaeology 32:3, 2001) — though the wreck preserves the lower hull only, so its machine silence is weak and is not leaned on. What decides is the tradition itself: Agius's Classic Ships of Islam (Brill 2008), the scholarly survey of this ocean's ships from the 7th to the 16th century, read whole this round, describes the anchors of every period — Omani stone anchors with sharp-ended timbers fitted through, Indo-Arabian stone shanks at Siraf (8th–11th c.), Ibn Sida's wood-and-lead anchor recipe (d. 1066), Correia's iron-and-stone and Varthema's marble anchors (16th c.) — each topped by a hawser hole and a rope, and names no winding machine in gear, crew roles or terminology anywhere in the book. At the tradition's best-documented end, the Gulf craft of the last working-sail century stow the anchor loose on deck or hang it on the kalba cat beam at the prow, take lines to bitts and the rumaana bollard, and acquire a winch only 'with the advent of power' (Lockerbie, catnaps.org, fetched whole). Unlike the junk (two primary texts), the panokseon (the living horong) and the corbita (her own trade's gear list), this tradition attests no machine at any era to extend from — drawing one would invent existence, form and place at once, the class of error the r172 Georgian capstan was. The record stays silent and the builder draws nothing. That her crew worked the grapnel by direct pull is itself an inference, marked as one on the card. Named as not fetched: Villiers' Sons of Sinbad (borrow-gated, search-inside blocked too), Vosmer's reconstruction chapter (403), the PSAS Jewel of Muscat paper (pay-gated), Agius's two other dhow books — any of them, fetched and attesting a sail-era machine, reopens the question. Scope: the judgment is for the drawn sewn trader and the sail tradition as documented; a powered conversion's winch is a different ship.

vessels.name: Chinese junk
rows: ⚠ **the battened lug is not original.** Junks carried SQUARE sails before the 12th century, then adopted the tanja sail and the fully battened rig from the southern seas
full-length battens hold the sail flatter than ideal in every wind, which **reduces** windward performance against other fore-and-aft rigs
discounted — such descriptions 'tend to greatly exaggerate dimensions, usually to twice or more of the actual lengths'
12 bulkheads, 13 watertight compartments; first documented by Zhu Yu, *Pingzhou Ketan*, by 1119
a pottery model from before the 1st c. AD carries the oldest known depiction — about a millennium before Europe. On a large junk it took up to 20 hands to work in a blow

the anchor of Xu Jing's own sentence (1124) in its excavated form: two shank timbers pegged together with cross battens, each sweeping out to a curved fluke point, and a stone wedged crosswise through the gap between them — the stone the weight and the stock at once, its projecting ends forcing a fluke down to bite; no iron in it anywhere. Drawn at the size of the one such anchor recovered still jointed, stone and arm together — 마도해역-212, off the Korean coast on the sea road Chinese traders sailed to Goryeo: stone 1.09 m and 84 kg by the report, the arm 1.49 m measured off the report's own scale drawing. Xu Jing's great anchor was likely heavier (stated in the record). It rides recovered on the foredeck, rolled onto one stone end and one fluke, the rattan cable bent round the mid batten and wound on the windlass. Two spare roving anchors of the same make (*youding*) went down beside it in heavy weather, and are not drawn: no stow is attested. The form has since been recovered aboard a ship of its own century: the Goryeo coaster excavated at Songho-ri, Haenam in 2023 — hull timber dated AD 1021–1158 — carried one half of such an anchor stowed inside the hull near the stern, a single oak timber cut as shank and fluke together, 1.495 m long with three square through-mortises and a seat groove for the stone, its printed length matching the 1.49 m measured off the 마도해역-212 drawing to half a centimetre
1,000 men — 600 sailors and 400 men-at-arms; 'from twelve down to three sails'
sailed from China round the Cape of Good Hope to the United States and England, 1846–48
vessels.text:
A seagoing hull with watertight transverse bulkheads, an axial sternpost rudder and the magnetic compass used at sea, each attested in China well before it appeared in Europe. The hull descends from tapering rafts rather than from the dugout.

⚠ The battened lug is the exception and is often miscounted among them. Junks carried square sails until about the 12th century and then adopted the tanja sail and the fully battened rig from the southern seas. The battens make the sail self-reefing and allow it to set flat. A junk therefore works to windward considerably better than a square rig, and with a smaller crew: reefing is done by lowering battens onto the boom from the deck. Instrumented comparisons put a junk at 75–80% of a Bermudan rig's windward performance.
vessels.cite: Needham, *Science and Civilisation in China* IV.3; Quanzhou ship excavation 1974; Junk Rig Association instrumented polars.

polar.rigNote: The battens do it: they make the sail self-reefing and let it set flat, so it beats a square rig to windward on a fraction of the crew — about 75–80% of Bermudan performance.

anchor.source: Worcester, Junks and Sampans of the Yangtze: coastal passages in a fair breeze

hull.windlassProvenance: The bow machine of her own tradition, eyewitness-attested at her own size and century. Xu Jing, Gaoli tujing (1124), ch. 34, on the Song sea ships (kezhou, ten-odd zhang): 'between the two cheek-posts at the ship's head there is a winch wheel, on which is wound a rattan cable as thick as a rafter, five hundred feet long; below hangs the anchor stone, two wooden flukes clamped at its sides ... getting under way, they roll the wheel up and recover it.' The Tiangong Kaiwu (1637) confirms the arrangement as standing practice: the yun che windlass winds the cable to raise the iron anchors, belayed to the two 'general's posts' at the brow of the bow. Station u 0.10 is a TEXT read (at the head, between the posts), +/-0.04 u — no plate, no plate scale. NO barrel dimension survives in either text: length 4.6 m is a GEOMETRIC class default (the barrel spans the foredeck between the posts; the drawn deck is 6.63 m wide at the drawn station, the audit's own measure), diameter 0.5 m and the 0.30 m underside height are CLASS DEFAULTS (Falconer 1769 cross-tradition, as r173's cog), post height 1.6 m a CLASS DEFAULT (the posts belay the cable, so they rise past the barrel). Needham IV.3 and Worcester were NOT fetched (access-restricted scans); this record cites the primaries directly.
hull.stoneAnchorProvenance: RECORDED, r199 (form and dimensions), on the r183 eyewitness warrant — the windlass's own load, from the same sentence that drew the machine (Xu Jing, Gaoli tujing 1124, ch. 34, warrant DIRECT: his kezhou is this hull's own size, class and century): 'below hangs the anchor-stone; on the stone's two sides it is clamped by two wooden hooks' (下垂矴石，石兩旁，夾以二木鈎), on a rattan cable thick as a rafter, no iron anywhere. THE FORM IS THE EXCAVATED ONE since r199: the two-shank stone-insert anchor (두 개의 닻채 사이에 닻돌을 끼어 넣고) of the 2017 마도해역 시굴조사 보고서 (국립해양문화재연구소, fetched and mined r198) — two cheek timbers pegged with cross battens, each sweeping outward to a curved fluke point, the stone wedged crosswise through the gap between their seat faces, its ends projecting both sides as the stock, forcing the fluke plane vertical on the bottom. The report itself reads the type as CHINESE practice — 마도해역-203 came up with one arm and a braided bamboo cable, the cordage it names Chinese, its stated analogue the anchor on the Eastern-Han pottery ship excavated at Dongjiao, Guangzhou, 1951 — and the Mado anchorage sits on the Goryeo west-coast sea road Xu Jing's own fleet sailed in 1123. The text's clause lands on the artifact exactly: the stone's two broad faces are what the two hook-timbers clamp, 石兩旁. A second stone records that grip in its own dressing (read r200, page verified by eye r201): 진도-621, the one Chinese-form stone at Myeongnyang (보고서 Ⅰ 2015, p. 447; report Ⅲ's synthesis names it direct evidence of a Chinese ship in the strait) — 175.6 × 22.8 × 13.2 cm, 108 kg, bar-form, symmetric, finely dressed, a 13 cm seat groove cut on BOTH broad faces (내외면) where the 닻채 timbers seat and ~4 cm grooves top and bottom for retaining pins (고정못) — the third measured insert stone after 203/206/212, and the first with the seat itself dimensioned. THE DRAWN OBJECT IS 마도해역-212 AT ITS OWN SIZE, the one find in the tradition where arm and stone survive as one object (raised 2014-08-01 still articulated, 결구된 채 — the report states this proves the insert structure). Stone: the report's printed record, 109 × 29 × 10 cm, 84 kg. Arm: no printed dimension exists, so the timber is MEASURED off the report's own 1/10 catalogue drawing (p. 210, rendered at 300 DPI, 4.06 px/cm against its printed 50 cm bar — the plate reproduces the stone's printed 29 cm width to 0.1 cm at the same scale, and the arm agrees across its three views to 0.3%): run 1.49 m tip to butt, section 0.16 × 0.15 m, the fluke sweeping 0.285 m off-axis over the outer 0.81 m and tapering to a ~0.07 m point, the stone seat a shallow 0.25 m waist cut 1.02–1.27 m from the tip (the plan's stone crossing reads 1.02–1.29 — joinery and plan agree, drawn at seat centre 1.15), three square mortises at 0.58, 0.90 and 1.37 m carrying the battens — Hong 2013's artifact ⑤, 'the Mado arm with three square holes', by its own excavation record. Assembly per the report's complete-form schematic (완형 추정 모식도, p. 205): seat faces inward the stone's thickness apart, the cable bent round the mid batten and led out between the horns. SCALE IS CONTESTED: 84 kg reads as a coastal trader's anchor, and the kezhou's great anchor — a four-man windlass, a 500-chi cable — likely swung heavier; the corpus's measured ceiling is 마도해역-203 (98 × 40 × 34 cm, 255 kg; = the 2023 닻돌 report's stone 052) with 마도해역-206 between (178 × 28 × 13 cm, 133 kg, an 18 cm 결구부 seat and retaining grooves cut mid-length). But no larger pair survives measured, a scaled-up 212 would be a derivation with an invented factor, and the record beats a derivation from the record — the smaller true object over the larger invented one, the gap stated here. The cable's 0.10 m diameter stays an INFERENCE from the text's simile (其大如椽), its 500-chi length the record's, not drawn whole. STOW is PLACEMENT INFERENCE: under way the anchor rides recovered (收之) on the open foredeck between the stem and its own windlass, head aft, cable to the barrel (上綰藤索); the assembly is cruciform in section — horns on one axis, the stone crossing the other — so it cannot lie flat, and it is drawn at repose, rolled onto one stone end and one horn, settled to the deck by measurement. The r183 hang finding stands: a hung anchor sits pocketed out of every broadside view behind this hull's bluff bow shell (raycast, r183), so a hang would be invisible and is not drawn. The text's two spare roving anchors (游矴) are NOT drawn: attested in use only, no stow named — drawing one would invent place. CORROBORATED IN PRINT, r203: the 송호리1호선 excavation report (해남, 국립해양유산연구소 2025; fetched whole from the institute's board, 35,320,352 bytes byte-exact) catalogues the form's one aboard-ship record in anything fetched here — one oak timber cut as 닻채 and 닻가지 together (the analysis report's species table reads its sample 42, named 닻가지, 상수리나무류), made to be joined face-to-face with an identical opposite half, printed at 최대길이 149.5 cm, 최대 폭 91.3, 최대두께 19.1 cm, 28 kg (p. 160, plate read by eye), with three through-stations in the shank and a 'ㄷ'-section groove between the lower two that the report reads as the stone's joint (닻돌 결합부(추정)) — found INSIDE the hull, port side near the stern, and the hull's own plank is radiocarbon-dated AD 1021–1158 (Beta Analytic 2σ; CAL 1040–1220; the dendro study fells the bark-bearing bottom plank at 1055–1085): Xu Jing's own century, on the same west-coast road at its Haenam turn. The printed 149.5 cm stands half a centimetre from the 1.49 m this record measures off 212's drawing, and the photographs show the three stations as square mortises — 212's own joint detail. Contested within that report and named here: its survey chapter calls the stations 나무못 구멍 (peg holes), its catalogue 관통 구멍 bound 줄로 (rope through-holes); 212's own halves are pegged with cross battens. And the carrier is a Korean-built 전통 한선 coaster, so the 2017 report's Chinese-practice reading widens — the form served both hull traditions on this coast — without unseating its cordage and analogue evidence. The ship's three catalogued 닻돌 (9.2, 151.3, 8.3 kg) are all grooved lashed-form; none is an insert-seat stone, and the anchor's own stone is not identified among them. The 151.3 kg stone's rock is contested between the site's own two reports — 역암 by the excavation catalogue, 화산력응회암 by the analysis report's petrology, which also prints different dimensions (133.6 × 55.8 × 16.7 cm vs 1,335 × 593 × 226 mm) — both stated.

five or six iron anchors is the *Tiangong kaiwu* inventory for the state grain ship — gear the text extends to the ocean transport whole — the mightiest the ‘house-guarding anchor’ of about 500 catties, two more worked at the head, two at the stern. The forging chapter gives the form: four claws made first, then joined section by section to the shank — no stock, no wood; whichever way it lands a claw bites. The sweep of the drawn claws follows the Penglai anchor's published drawing, which carries its own scale: each arm leaves the shank foot nearly flat and turns up to its point at a third of the anchor's length out from the shank. No text gives a size: the drawn lengths — 1.86 m the sheet, 1.57 m the rest — are scaled by weight from the complete Ming anchor excavated at the Penglai naval fortress in 1984, 2.15 m and 456 kg. The bow-worked three lie recovered on the foredeck, cables to the general’s-posts and the windlass barrel; the stern pair lies on the poop’s own top deck — the aft working surface the sheets too are worked from — each cable flaked in a coil beside it, for the belay no text records. The drawn iron weighs what the record weighs: each anchor's member thickness is solved from its recorded weight — the sheet's 500 catties, the calibrator's 456 kg — with shank-to-claw proportions from a calipered anchor the same harbour's 2005 dredge raised. The solved sheet carries a shank 13 cm through at the crown and claws of 10 cm.
vessels.text:
**The famous dimensions come from a novel.** The 44-zhang figure appears first in Luo Maodeng's *Xiyang Ji* of 1597 — a work of fiction written 164 years after the last voyage, in which ships are built with divine assistance — and was carried into the *Ming Shi* when that was compiled in 1739.

Two physical arguments cut against it. A length-to-beam ratio of 2.5 is a barge, not a seagoing hull; and unreinforced wooden hulls hog beyond about 90 m, which is why the longest wooden ship ever built needed iron strapping and still leaked continuously. Then the decisive one: the Longjiang shipyard was excavated in 2003–04 and its largest building basin is **421 m long and 41 m wide** — narrower than the 52 m beam the ships are supposed to have had.

The hull drawn here is at the defensible length. The claimed length is shown as an outline beside it, because the claim is part of the history even though it is almost certainly wrong.
vessels.cite: Church, *Monumenta Serica* 53 (2005); Sleeswyk, *Nautical Research Journal* (1996); Xin Yuan'ou; Longjiang shipyard excavation 2003–04.

hull.windlassProvenance: A FLEET-CLASS EXTENSION, not a ship attestation — this hull's own record attests no fitting (her attestation is 'generated'). What is attested is the tradition: the Tiangong Kaiwu (1637) names the yun che windlass that 'winds the cable and raises the anchor' on the state grain ships (five or six iron anchors, two worked at the head, cable belayed to the two general's-posts at the brow of the bow), and says of the sea transports 'the gear is all the same' (qi ju jie tong) — and that sea transport, the zheyang ship, is the carrier of the Yuan and EARLY MING state fleets, the treasure fleet's own era and administration. Position at the bow between the posts follows Xu Jing (1124). Station u 0.10 TEXT read +/-0.05. NO dimension is a source read: barrel 6.0 m is a GEOMETRIC class default (a third of beam; the foredeck at the station is at least 10.48 m wide — a conservative probe of the drawn shell), diameter 0.6 m is the Kiel cog's measured barrel carried as a CLASS DEFAULT, post height 1.8 m a CLASS DEFAULT. The TGK is 200 years after the voyages and localizes the machine by naming the bow posts, not in one sentence — the join is stated in build/staging/r174/JUDGMENT.md.
hull.ironAnchorProvenance: DRAWN, r184 — a FLEET-CLASS EXTENSION, the same join as the windlass: this hull's own record attests no fitting (attestation 'generated'). The Tiangong Kaiwu (1637, ~200 years after the voyages — the gap named) carries the object in two chapters. Zhouche counts the inventory for the state grain ship: five or six iron anchors, the mightiest the kanjia mao (sheet anchor) at about 500 catties RECORDED, two worked at the head, two at the stern, cables belayed to the two general’s-posts and broken out by the yun-che windlass; and ‘the ocean transport’s gear is all the same’ (qi ju jie tong) carries the set to the zheyang ship, the Yuan and early-Ming state sea carrier (the r174 join, build/staging/r174/JUDGMENT.md). Chuiduan gives the FORM, fetched whole r184 (Gutenberg #25273, staging/r184): the forging method first makes the FOUR CLAWS, then joins them section by section to the shank — no stock, no wood, the largest thing under furnace and hammer. NO dimension is in any text; a measured surviving four-claw anchor now sets the scale (r188 — the replacement this field promised). 蓬莱水城出土 1984 — the complete excavated Ming four-claw anchor from the Penglai naval fortress, 全長 2.15 m at 456 kg (Matsui 2013 fig. 3 caption, after 王冠倬 2000: 149, 277–278; the paper local since r187, its fig. 3 read on the plate r188) — calibrates weight to length by cube-law within the one tradition: the 500-catty (~295 kg) sheet lands at 1.86 m full length; the pair’s 300 catties — still an INFERENCE at the forging text’s own anvil threshold, the text records only the sheet’s weight — at 1.57 m, carried to the stern pair whose weight is not recorded. The record fields carry the FULL crown-to-ring length a find’s 全長 measures (the r187 yotsume convention; the drawn ring top lands at the field’s value). Cross-check: 泉州四湖港出土 1981, 残高 2.68 m at 758.3 kg — incomplete, its missing parts dotted in the figure, weighing less than the ~880 kg cube-law gives a complete 2.68 m: a consistent lower bound. Sensitivity NAMED: fig. 3b, 山東省梁山県宋金河出土 1956, 全長 1.36 m, the shank inscribed 「甲字五百六十号 八十五斤 洪武五年」 — an as-made 85 catties (~50 kg) in 1372, the corpus’s slender small-craft build at less than half Penglai’s weight per length; a power law through both dated Ming points would give 1.96 m sheet (inside the audit’s 12% band) and 1.77 m pair (at the band’s edge). Penglai — the naval-fortress find of the state build the forging text describes — is the calibrator for a state ship’s tackle; the choice moves the drawn anchor by a hand’s width and is recorded here. Claw sweep MEASURED r189, from the calibrator's own drawing — fig. 3a self-scales, 全長 2.15 m in its caption; the plate read at 322.8 px/m from a 300-DPI render (build/staging/r189). The drawing is 王冠倬's published line drawing of a corroded find, so the proportions carry its draughting precision, not a survey's. The pair drawn widest is read as in-plane; the two sides give reach 0.325/0.354 of 全長 and tip height 0.222/0.181 — the spread is the obliquity bound — and the means set the class: tips at 0.339 of 全長 from the shank axis, 0.201 above the crown centre, the arm leaving the shank foot near-flat and turning up to ~40° at the point, arm sections tapering 0.024 → 0.009 of 全長, the head a small forged eye 0.062 across in place of the drawn wide ring, the crown ball 0.078 — its bottom, the datum 全長 measures from, 0.039 below the claw joins. The audit holds the drawn reach to the measured proportion (V-SWEEP) and the crown-bottom-to-ring-top span to the field itself (V-LEN). Cable material RECORDED in the same chapter: anchor cables are split green bamboo strip, boiled then twisted (po xi qing mie) — hemp is the text’s sail and towing cordage, not the anchor’s. Drawn recovered, all five (r185): the bow-worked three on the foredeck, cables to the general's-posts and the barrel; the stern pair (shao yong er zhi — stations RECORDED) on the poop's top-tier roof, the surface MEASURED r185 (ray map, build/staging/r185): continuous u 0.68–1.00 at sheer + 4.18 m, ~11 m clear abeam at the stern stations, and already the drawn ship's aft working deck — the after-sheets are worked from it. The stern pair's weight is NOT RECORDED (qi yu — 'the rest'): the head pair's 300-catty inference at the forging text's own anvil threshold carries over, shank 2.0 m. The stern BELAY is in no text — the jiangjunzhu sentence names the bow posts — so each stern cable is drawn bent to its ring and flaked in a coil beside it, a stow, not an invented lead (the r182 grapnel standing). Stow spots PLACEMENT INFERENCE, measured and iterated (r182/r183 method). Member sections MASS-SOLVED r190: the r189 sections followed the plate's line weights and summed to 156 kg of wrought iron against the find's captioned 456 — a third of the record — so sections now come from the balance itself. The section RATIOS are a caliper record from the same harbour: the 2005 second dredge of the same basin raised a complete four-claw anchor, and the excavation brief (蓬莱3艘古船发掘简报 §7, haijiaoshi.com/archives/425, saved r190) measures it — shank 177 cm at ⌀8.5 cm, claws 73 cm at ⌀7 cm, one diameter over the claw's length, tips 144 cm apart, a head eye ⌀4.5, forge marks named on the surface. The absolute scale is solved per anchor so the drawn iron weighs the record's own mass at 7850 kg/m³ — the weight fields sheetKg 295 (RECORDED, the text's 500 catties), bowerKg/sternKg 177 (the standing 300-catty inference). At the calibrator, 456 kg draws shank ⌀15.5→11.9 cm and claw ⌀11.3→6.8 cm on 2.15 m; all three record anchors share one density class, so they solve to one proportion set and the r188 cube-law stands. The method checks itself against the calipers: the 2005 anchor's own members integrate to ~170 kg, and handing that mass and its ~1.94 m length back to the solve returns claw ⌀7.1 cm against the measured 7.0 and shank ⌀9.7 against 8.5. The claw centreline, crown ball and head eye stay the plate's (r189): a line drawing carries a silhouette, and only the sections were its line weights'. The audit holds each drawn anchor's integrated iron to its record's weight (V-MASS, 12%).

vessels.text:
Flat-bottomed so it could take the ground on a tidal flat and be unloaded at low water, which is what the Hanse ports needed. It also carries the **pintle-and-gudgeon stern rudder**, first depicted on the Winchester font about 1180 — the single most important European ship fitting of the Middle Ages.

A replica was instrumented and the result is sobering: in a gentle breeze it made good 74–76° to the true wind with a velocity made good of 0.15 knots. In twenty knots of wind it lost ground.
vessels.cite: Bremen cog, Deutsches Schiffahrtsmuseum; Brandt & Hochkirch 1995 replica trials.

polar.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

hull.sternProvenance: Sharp-sterned on a straight raked post: the Bremen cog is double-ended, her planking closing on stem and sternpost (Lahn Blatt 9 elevation; the DSM booklet: 'vorn und achtern gerade Steven auf einer flachen Kielplanke'). transom 0 from r214 — the 0.3 it replaced drew a flat stern face above water that no plate supports. The castle's stern beams overhang the post; the hull does not.
hull.windlassProvenance: The wreck's own machine. The reconstructed Bremen cog carries a windlass athwartships UNDER THE AFTCASTLE DECK, forward of the helmsman — Ellmers (DSM, Drassana): 'the man at the tiller had to stand ... behind the heavy windlass' — with a separate capstan (Gangspill) on the castle top, NOT drawn (residual r173). Dimensions are the Kiel replica's build record to the DSM's own Lahn plans: Bratspill 4.5 m long, 60 cm thick (Baykowski 1991, via de.wikipedia Bremer Kogge — TEXT reads, no plate scale applies). Station u 0.875 is Ellmers's 'in its middle' applied to the castle's RECORDED run (r214: the plan's 8.2 m from u 0.70 to the after edge at 1.02, so its middle is x 8.1 m abaft midships, u 0.875 by the loft); before r214 it was a text read of 0.82 against a guessed run. Precision is the overhang read's, ±0.02 u. Barrel underside 0.30 m over the deck, the eight-square barrel, two standards and two shipped handspikes are CLASS DEFAULTS from Falconer 1769 WINDLASS ('holes bored through the body', 'lower part ... about a foot above the deck'), named cross-tradition. The aftcastle over the machine is drawn as of r205 (see castleProvenance); the barrel keeps its attested place beneath the castle deck. Whether the ORIGINAL barrel was among the >2,000 recovered pieces is not established by the sources fetched in r173; the claim is the reconstruction and the replicas, not the find inventory. The Gangspill on the castle top is drawn from r212 (see capstanProvenance).
hull.castleProvenance: The wreck's own structure, and from r214 its own PLAN. The Bremen cog's aftcastle is preserved to its highest rail and stands whole on the reconstructed ship; Ellmers (Drassana, r173): 'a windlass in its middle and a capstan on its top', the man at the tiller 'underneath the castle-deck in between the long cabins at both sides and behind the heavy windlass'. PLAN, RECORD numbers (Westphal, DAS LOGBUCH 27/1991 H.4 p.128, the Kiel replica's build report citing Lahn, Das Achterkastell der Hansekogge, Deutsche Schiffahrt 1/1979): an after part trapezoidal in plan, 4.75 m long, 7.20 m broad at its forward edge and 6.50 m at its after edge, plus two side parts each 3.45 m long and 1.65 m broad; the castle deck cross-planked over fore-and-aft beams, those on athwartship beams on vertical posts; the castle overhangs the main deck aft and at both sides, so the after posts stand on two stern beams (Heckbalken), the forward of which is propped amidships; the starboard side wall's lower part three stringer-like timbers and a plank, its upper part 17 vertical boards (counted from nail traces, three boards found). Before 1978 the reconstruction assumed a simple open platform; the wall fragments overturned that, which is why the r205 open parapet is replaced by walls. PLATE READ, Lahn Blatt 9 elevation at 60 px/m (Tanner & Belasus 2021 fig. 1, r213): the castle's after edge stands about 0.5 m abaft the sternpost's after face at the castle deck's height (±0.2 m), which is 0.7 m abaft the post's after face where it meets the top strake, the post raking about 0.4 m per metre of height there — overhangAftM 0.7 is measured from the strake, where the stern beams lie, the castle deck is level, and the whole 8.2 m reads as one deck line — so the side parts are wings at the castle deck's own level along each side, the main deck open between them; the Roland von Bremen replica photographed from the quarter (r213/roland-ubena.jpg) shows exactly that: vertical-boarded walls on beam ends overhanging stern and sides, narrow decked wings forward with lower walls. PHOTOGRAPH READS, no scale: the wing walls stand about 0.6 of the after part's wall; the after end is walled like the sides. CLASS DEFAULTS, named: 1.95 m from afterdeck to castle deck at the helmsman's station (the castle deck is set level there); the parapet 1.0 m; beams sided ~0.2 m, the Heckbalken 0.26; the lower wall 0.6 m deep; open rails on the wings' inner edges and forward ends and the breastrail over the open deck (no wall is recorded there); the two long cabins under the after part. fromU/toU are now DERIVED from the plan (the forward end at u 0.70, the after edge at 1.03, past the post) and kept in the record only for the builders that read them. The DSM booklet gives the ship as 7.02 m high to the winch on the castle deck; Lahn's elevation reads the castle deck about 5.4 m over the keel's underside. This model's castle deck stands about a metre higher over the water than that, because the model lays the cog's main deck at the sheer where the real deck lies a bulwark's height below it — a residual named in r214, not a castle fault. Lahn 1992 (Schriften des DSM 30) carries the castle sheets themselves — NOT fetched; a fetched plate would supersede the reads above. No forecastle: the wreck has none (Westphal, note 2), and none is drawn.
hull.capstanProvenance: The wreck's own capstan. The Gangspill was recovered WITH the Bremen cog from the Weser in the 1960s and is in the Deutsches Schiffahrtsmuseum's collection, Inv. I/11066/14 (museum-digital:bremen, object 3): oak, D 56 cm, H 176 cm — both RECORD numbers, the museum's own measurements of the recovered timber. The form is the museum's description: the rope ran round the lower wooden cone ('Das Windentau lief um den unteren Holzkegel') and the handspikes shipped into rectangular holes through the body above it; the museum says it was used to work the square sail round to the wind. Position: Ellmers (DSM, Drassana) — the aftcastle carries 'a windlass in its middle and a capstan on its top' — so it stands on the castle deck; atU 0.875 is 'its middle' applied to the castle's recorded plan (r214, see castleProvenance), ±0.02 u; Lahn's Blatt 9 elevation draws the Gangspill nearer the castle's forward end, about 1 m abaft it — a plate read at 60 px/m that contradicts the text by some 3 m, left with the text because the elevation cannot say which side of the centreline the machine stands on and the forward 3.45 m of the castle is two wings with open deck between. The head/cone split (head a little over half the height), the cone's neck (about 40 cm under the shoulder) and the head's breadth (a squared eight-sided block wider than the neck) are READS off the museum's oblique photograph, which carries no scale; the two through-shipped handspikes and the step under the foot are class defaults — the record does not give the count of holes. The Kiel replica's build record (Baykowski 1991) lists the Gangspill finished beside the Bratspill in 1987.
hull.rudderProvenance: The wreck's own irons. One of two RUDERÖSEN (rudder gudgeons) recovered with the Bremen cog is in the Deutsches Schiffahrtsmuseum, Inv. I/10393/08 (museum-digital:bremen object 22): iron, L×B×H 35 × 30 × 13 cm, a short tube with a massive clamp forged to it whose rectangular plates clasp the sternpost; the museum's text says four were needed to hang the rudder and that the blade must have carried downward pintles to drop into them — so hangings 4 is a RECORD number, and the pintle-on-blade, gudgeon-on-post arrangement is the record's. Ellmers (DSM, Drassana, r173): the two upper gudgeons were never nailed on, so the cog sank unfinished with her rudder not yet hung — the blade itself is NOT among the finds. The blade's form is Lahn's reconstruction, Blatt 9 elevation at 1:20 (reproduced as Tanner & Belasus 2021 fig. 1, Archaeonautica 21, CC BY, fetched r213 at 60 px/m): a narrow blade parallel to the raked sternpost from the post's heel to the castle's after beam, four hangings ticked along it, the tiller level forward under the castle deck. Chords are READS off that plate at 60 px/m: 0.60 m at the foot, 0.45 m at the head, ±0.15 m — the plate cannot support better. Tiller station u 0.90 is a TEXT read of Ellmers (the man at the tiller stood behind the windlass, which is at u 0.875 since r214), ±0.04 u; its height is the castle deck's underside less the beam and a hand's clearance, a class default. Stock siding (three quarters of the post's), the number and taper of the back pieces, strap breadth and the pintle knuckle's size are class defaults named in buildTimberRudder; the clamp plate's 35 cm on the post is the recovered iron's own length. vessels.text:
A small, shallow, weatherly hull carrying two or three lateen sails. Its significance is its ability to sail to windward: a square-rigged cog could run down to Guinea on the north-east trades but could not return against them, whereas a caravel could work back.

What it made possible has a name: the ***volta do mar***, the turn of the sea. To come home from West Africa you do not beat up the coast against the trades. You stand out **west** into the middle of the Atlantic, as far as the Azores, pick up the westerlies at 35–40°N and run home on them. Sailing away from your destination in order to reach it is the first great piece of applied knowledge about the wind field, and in 1500 Cabral's southern version of it swung so far west that it reached Brazil.
vessels.cite: Portuguese *Regimento* c. 1509; Barros, *Décadas da Ásia*.

vessels.text:
A three- or four-masted ocean-going ship developed in Portugal and Spain during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, carvel-built, with a forecastle forward and a high rounded stern carrying an aftcastle. It carried cargo and guns on the same voyage and was large enough to remain stable in heavy seas.

The rig is mixed: square sails on the fore and main for driving power, a lateen mizzen aft to help the ship steer and lie closer to the wind. A typical three-master set six sails — spritsail, foresail, mainsail, mizzen and two topsails.

Portuguese carracks on the India run were often over 1,000 tons. Galleons gradually superseded the type from the late sixteenth century, though carracks remained in use into the middle of the seventeenth.

vessels.text:
The standard Mediterranean warship for four hundred years after gunpowder, and the ship that fought Lepanto — about 400 of them on one afternoon in October 1571, the largest galley action ever fought.

Her armament faces FORWARD. The heavy gun sits on the centreline at the bow, aimed by aiming the ship, and it fired once — at fifty metres or less, immediately before boarding. The broadside that was re-organising Atlantic warfare in the same century has no place here: the sides are full of oars.

The dimensions of a fighting fact: 42 m of hull carries only 1.1 m of freeboard, so the rowing frame — the *apostis*, the rectangular outrigger the oars actually pivot on — stands wider than the hull itself, and the spur at the bow is a boarding bridge, not a ram. At Lepanto the two systems of rowing met: Venice still rowed *alla sensile*, three separate oars to a bench; Spain and Genoa had gone *a scaloccio*, one great oar pulled by three to five men. Everyone converted after the battle, because a scaloccio can be rowed by chained men and sensile cannot.

Guilmartin's central measurement is logistical: a galley dashes at 7 knots for twenty minutes, cruises at 3–4, and carries water for a few days at most — 150 rowers working in a Mediterranean summer drink tons of it. Galley war is therefore amphibious war, fought port to port along coasts, and it ended not when sailing ships got better guns but when the round ship could finally keep the sea in winter.
vessels.cite: Guilmartin, *Gunpowder and Galleys* (rev. ed., Naval Institute Press, 2003); Morrison (ed.), *The Age of the Galley* (Conway, 1995).

vessels.text:
A merchant great galley's hull converted into a floating battery — the heaviest thing under oars in the sixteenth-century Mediterranean, and the type that opened Lepanto. Venice built her out of the reserve of galee grosse, the three-masted merchant galleys that had carried the Flanders and Levant trades, and the six that the Arsenal finished converting in 1570–71 fought at the front of the Christian line on 7 October 1571.

Structurally she inverts the war galley's one hard constraint. A galia sottile carries her whole battery at the bow because her sides at gun height are full of oars. The great galley's hull is deep enough to carry a second deck clear over the rowers' heads, spanning the full width of the rowing frame, and the guns stand on that deck and fire outboard over the oars — eight or nine pieces a side, with the five-piece heavy battery at the bow and chasers aft, about thirty guns in all. Her freeboard, about 2.8 m to the gun deck against a galley's 1.1, means a galley alongside cannot board her without climbing.

At Lepanto the six galleasses were towed into position in pairs ahead of the Christian line, and the Ottoman fleet had to row past them to come to grips. Their fire — the first sustained heavy-gun bombardment an Ottoman galley fleet had ever taken from shipboard — sank or damaged a number of galleys and, what mattered more, broke up the dressing of the Ottoman line before contact. Guilmartin's judgment is that the galleasses did not win the battle by gunfire; they disordered the attack that the Christian galleys then destroyed at close quarters.

She was too heavy to row effectively — about three knots in a burst, towed whenever the fleet manoeuvred — and depended on her lateen rig for passage. Spain sent four galleasses of the Naples squadron with the 1588 Armada, where one, Girona, was wrecked on the Antrim coast with some 1,300 men lost. Venice kept galleasses in commission into the early eighteenth century, but the broadside's future belonged to the pure sailing ship, which carried more guns further on a fraction of the crew.
vessels.cite: Guilmartin, *Gunpowder and Galleys* (rev. ed., Naval Institute Press, 2003); Morrison (ed.), *The Age of the Galley* (Conway, 1995).

vessels.text:
The standard warship of the Joseon navy from 1555 until the nineteenth century, and the ship Yi Sun-sin fought every battle of the Imjin War with. The name means "board-roofed ship": above the oar deck the shipwrights built a second, higher deck on stanchions — the sangjang — walled with heavy plank, so that the whole fighting crew stands a full storey above the water behind timber, with the commander's roofed tower rising amidships. The first was launched in 1555, after the Eulmyo wako raid of that year showed the old single-decked ships could be boarded and taken.

Her construction is the Korean coastal tradition scaled up to war burden. The bottom is dead flat, built of thick pine planks edge-fastened with oak pegs and locked by massive crossbeams whose ends pierce the hull sides — no iron nails, and no keel. A flat bottom suits a coast with some of the world's largest tides: she takes the ground upright when the water leaves, and she turns nearly in her own length, pivoting on it. The price is speed. Fifty to sixty rowers working eight to ten great sculling oars drove perhaps three knots, and both fleets' accounts agree the Japanese ships were faster through the water.

The two navies of the Imjin War (1592–1598) disagreed about what a warship is for. The Japanese fleet — atakebune and the lighter sekibune — carried arquebusiers and swordsmen, and fought by coming alongside and boarding; its lightly framed hulls mounted few heavy guns, because they could not bear the recoil. The panokseon is the opposite argument built in timber: heavy cannon — the cheonja, jija, hyeonja and hwangja chongtong, throwing iron shot and the great fletched daejanggunjeon to several hundred metres — worked from behind a high plank bulwark that boarders would have to climb. Joseon squadrons stood off, fired, and dismasted or holed the boarders before they could close. The geobukseon, the famous turtle ship, is this same hull with the fighting deck roofed over completely.

Her hardest test came after her navy was nearly destroyed. At Chilcheollyang in August 1597 a Joseon fleet under Won Gyun was annihilated — and thirteen panokseon survived. With those thirteen, reinstated to command, Yi Sun-sin met the Japanese advance fleet of 133 warships in the Myeongnyang strait on 26 October 1597, where a tidal race runs to ten knots and reverses. Anchored across the narrows against the flood, his line fought until the tide turned, then drove the disordered Japanese van back through the strait onto their own supports. About thirty Japanese ships were destroyed; no panokseon was lost. The type, continued as the jeonseon of the late Joseon fleet, remained the kingdom's standard warship until the navy itself was reorganised out of existence in the 1890s.
vessels.cite: Hong Sun-jae, 'Understanding the Structure of the Panokseon' (*Military History* 135, 2025); Hawley, *The Imjin War* (RAS Korea, 2005); Underwood, *Korean Boats and Ships* (1934). No panokseon survives; every dimension here is a reconstruction from the documentary record and is labelled derived where it is inference. The 1795 전서 도설 spec is read at 300 dpi from 국립해양유산연구소, 『거북선 학술 복원 보고서 문헌편』 (학술총서 91집); the turtle-ship design figures (통제영 상장 33–33.8척 and 전라좌수영 27.8척, both over a 27척 upper hull) from the same institute's 『거북선 학술 복원 보고서 본문편』 (학술총서 91집, 2026).

The marines and gunners fight from it a full storey above the water; the rowers work beneath it, under cover. Before 1555 a Korean warship had one deck and could be boarded; this second one is the answer.
