hull.towerProvenance: The FORM is attested: the Gakseon dobon jeonseon drawing — the late-Joseon plate this card's own image follows — draws the janggundae as an open pavilion on the fighting deck: a railed platform on posts under a hipped roof standing clear above the bulwarks, the commander visible from the whole squadron. The PLAN is derived: no panokseon survives, so the 3.2 m square, the 2.6 m platform height and the roof pitch are read off that drawing at ship scale — good to the nearest half metre, no finer. The ladder, the baluster spacing and every scantling are reconstruction: a pavilion whose platform can be reached and whose rails land on its own columns, drawn at the joinery any standing structure needs; the plate attests none of it piece by piece.
hull.portProvenance: The PORTS are attested for the class: the panokseon's chongtong stood on the fighting deck and fired through its plank bulwark — the gunners loading behind cover is the argument of the walled deck itself, and her card's Guns row carries the attested battery. The COUNT AT THE WALL, SIZE and SILL HEIGHT are derived: no example survives, the late-Joseon jeonseon plate on her card resolves the sangjang band's port row but not the fighting-deck wall's, and six a side is the drawn split of the recorded dozen-plus pieces. Each port is drawn 0.52 m square with its sill 0.14 m over the fighting deck — low, so the muzzle clears its own timber bed. Since round 141 the ports are OPENINGS cut through the drawn plank, with reveal faces the plank's own thickness deep and a dark board behind each so the port frames its muzzle in shadow; before that each was a dark plate laid on the wall's face with the barrel passing through solid plank.
hull.anchorProvenance: The 닻 the warship plate itself draws: her navy's album, the Gakseondobon (c. 1797), lists mast, anchor [碇], oars and rudder on the 전선 plate (encykorea E0000455) — the anchor's presence is the album's own, one step more direct than the horong, which the album carries only on the grain-ship plate. The FORM is the tradition's, a NAVY-TRADITION EXTENSION stated here: the West Sea composite of oak shank (닻채), hook-arms hung both sides (닻가지), and a long grooved rectangular anchor-stone (닻돌) lashed on, because oak alone will not sink — the stone serving as the stock, 석제 닻장 in the report's own words. The type is RECORDED on her own coast: 154 anchor stones off Taean and Incheon, 2008–2019, rope grooves cut for the lashing, the wooden anchors found with them radiocarbon-dated from the 2nd century BC through Joseon — her own dynasty inside the run (Korea Heritage Service 2021). The stone is RECORDED since r201, the excavated object at its own size (the r199 rule): 진도Ⅳ-58 / 명량21-17, raised from the Myeongnyang strait's grid D10 on 14 August 2021 and catalogued at 166 × 53 × 29 cm, 458 kg, its lashing grooves cut top and bottom — 폭 7 × 깊이 2.5 cm and 11 × 3.5 cm — and its rim dressed (치석) toward the rectangle (『진도 명량대첩로 해역 수중발굴조사 보고서 Ⅳ』 2024, p. 147; caption verified against the plate's own photographs on the rendered page, r200). It is the largest Korean lashed-form stone in any report fetched here, raised from the same water that gave the class its arm, and it sits inside the corpus's own large band — Hong 2012's 대형군, 304–590 kg / 146–263 cm, the classification the 2021 Mado report itself applies (its footnote 64) — replacing the exhibition threshold this record cited through r200 ('over 2 m, 300–700 kg', Taean 2021). The band's ceiling runs to 590 kg, so larger stones are attested in the corpus; none fetched carries its own catalogue entry above 458, and that gap is stated. At 458 kg the stone is a load the drawn four-man horong breaks out at its bars' purchase. The ARMS take the form study's own count and splay (r196): TWO — every stock-anchor Hong 2013 draws carries two (그림 16 forms A–D, the stone-stock schematic 그림 17, and all six artifact reconstructions on p.135), and the institute's reconstruction figure draws two limbs at staggered whipped stations. The pre-r196 four came from the Standard Korean Dictionary's '보통 네 갈고리이며 두 갈고리도 있다' — CONTESTED here: the study reserves the many-hooked form for the STOCKLESS anchor (its E, whose modern analogue it names in 그림 18, a four-claw grapnel), never the stock anchor this record draws. SPLAY is MEASURED, 0.38 rad from the shank — the mean of six limb chords read tip-to-root at 300 DPI (그림 16 (A) 22°/27°, (C) 19°/26°, the institute figure ~19°/17°; the 17–27° spread is the audit band) — replacing the pre-r196 drawn 0.78, twice any plate. The ARM TIMBER is RECORDED (r197): 진도-641, the lashed tradition's one recovered wooden arm published with dimensions (the board's 2025 송호리1호선 report prints a second dimensioned anchor timber — a whole one-piece oak half of the two-shank insert form, 149.5 cm — a different form, named below) — raised off Jindo's Myeongnyang strait, zone C, 3 September 2013, and catalogued in 『진도 명량대첩로 해역 수중발굴조사 보고서 Ⅰ』 (국립해양문화재연구소 2015, p. 467; fetched whole from the institute's report board): 길이 190 cm, 너비 19.6 cm, 두께 40 cm, oak (수종분석: 상수리나무류). The catalogue's measured drawing reproduces its own printed numbers against the 1 m bar at 8.79 px/cm — plans 188.7/189.0 cm long and 19.2/20.7 cm wide, side envelope 40.7 cm — so the plate supports centimetre precision and the class draws the arm at the record: the whole timber, root to carved point, 1.90 m, section 0.196 m, replacing the pre-r197 drawn defaults (hook limb 1.2, section 0.12). The 두께 40 is the root crook's side envelope — the timber sweeps up where it met the shank — and the drawn frame keeps the institute figure's straight crossed timbers, the curve named. The species is not the tradition's only one: the strait's second arm — 진도Ⅱ-328, a 59.4 × 9.2 cm fragment raised 5 June 2017, the catalogue's own 목제닻을 구성하는 일부분 (보고서 Ⅱ 2018, p. 336) — analyses as zelkova (느티나무; the report's species appendix names its sample by the same date and grid), so the tradition built its arms in at least two hardwoods; a broken remnant, it tests nothing the class draws, and 진도-641 stays the only whole-run record. CONTESTED, the joint: 진도-641's two peg stations sit 0.35–0.55 m from its lap-notched root end, the economy of Hong's foot-rooted variant, not the drawn crossed frame's ~0.79 m derived blunt limb; the institute's frame stays the drawn one (r194's declared source), the artifact's own stations carried here. The Gwangyang arm (artifact ⑥) remains undimensioned in print — the form study's catalogue is qualitative and a reported find has no excavation report; its plain white photo rod anchors no scale. VARIANT NAMED: Hong's own plates root the arms at the foot with carved points rising to the stock's height, while the institute's figure crosses them whipped at 0.35 with points down and blunt ends bracing the stone — the drawn frame follows the institute's, the study's variant stated. The SHANK is DERIVED (r195): about 3.3 m on the 1.66 m stone, by the institute figure's own stone/shank proportion 0.51 (measured on the press-kit reconstruction at 3x, r194/r195), with the mechanism named in the form study the report itself cites — 홍광희 2013, 「전통 나무닻의 생김새 연구」, 『해양문화재』 6, pp. 107–143 (국립해양문화재연구소; fetched whole from the institute's own journal board, r195): the wooden anchor's shank was made LONG against oak's buoyancy, with the stock set at the arms' top height, not at the cable end where a modern anchor wears it. By that same study the pre-r195 crossbar is REMOVED: it sat at the modern head station the study explicitly distinguishes from the tradition's, and beside a stone stock the study argues a wooden 닻장 is redundant and draws none — the institute's reconstruction figure draws none either. CONTESTED, the study's own footnote 8: some hold that stock and stone were fitted together so the stone could not spin on a round shank — named here, not drawn. The crossings are pinned with two treenails each: the 19th-century 표민대화 anchor is drawn with two 나무못 at the joint, and both separately-made arms so far recovered (Jindo; Gwangyang Seonso) carry two square peg holes apiece — the study's artifacts ④ and ⑥. The stone's station and the frame are the institute's own reconstruction now (r194): the 2023 report 『한국의 닻돌』 (국립해양문화재연구소, 연구보고서 vol. 3, 195 pp., fetched whole from the CHA publications board, nttId 87406) names lashing to the shank's OUTSIDE (닻채 외부에 묶는 방식) the leading use for the plank-form stones, and carries the 19th-century 『표민대화』 fixing the stone at the shank's MIDDLE — 닻채 중앙부, held there by a 방살 pin through the shank (the pin is that book's own device; the drawn lashing is rope alone and the variant is named here). The institute's reconstruction figure (닻돌 구성, its Dec 2023 press release, fetched at 583×674 px — an unscaled illustration, proportions only) draws the crossed-arm frame whipped at the shank, blunt upper arm ends bracing the stone's underside, a spreader board across the splay, and the stone's centre at 0.57 of the shank above the foot; drawn at 0.55, band ±0.12 carrying the illustration's precision and the head-call (V-WSTATION audits the drawn station). The lashing follows the institute's reproduction as the 2021 exhibition poster photographs it: end turns seated in the stone's own rope grooves, crossed frapping over the midbody. The drawn rig is the one that HELD at sea (r196, mined from the thesis behind the study — 홍광희 2012, 조선대, fetched r195): in the thesis's own anchoring trials off Taean (표 8; 5–20 m of water, 30 m of cable, three runs per rig), only the stone lashed athwart the shank's middle anchored the boat — all three runs, at 33, 62 and 78 m — while the bare wooden anchor, the stone hung at the head and the stone hung on the cable failed all nine runs between them; the head rig floats the anchor so the arms cannot reach bottom (표 11's own reading), and the trial notes the wooden stock did little beside the stone — the crossbar's removal (r195) confirmed in the water. The cable-hung stone the thesis keeps as a plausible AUXILIARY for strong current, a second small stone bent to the cable — named here, not drawn. CONTESTED, the report's own sentence: no stone has been confirmed still lashed to its shank (닻돌이 닻채에 묶인 상태로 확인된 사례가 없어 추측만) — the station is the record's reconstruction, not a find; the boatwright's Chinese cognate (마광남, 배목수이야기 42) stands beside it. The one stone recovered still JOINTED to its timber (마도해역-212, raised articulated 2014, 2017 시굴보고서) is the Chinese two-shank INSERT form, pegged through mortised battens — a different joint, so the Korean lashed form's sentence stands (r199) — and that insert form is now attested aboard a Korean-built Goryeo coaster (송호리1호선, Haenam, hull dated AD 1021–1158, excavation report 2025: one oak half, 149.5 cm printed, stowed inside the hull), so the form crossed hull traditions without touching the lashed form's own evidence. Stow is PLACEMENT INFERENCE, the fleet rule: under way the anchor lies recovered on the open foredeck beside its own horong, rolled so no member stands upright, the cable bent at the head and led to the barrel. The boatwright's trip-ring and buoy are a fishing practice with no warship warrant — not drawn. No fetched source draws a 16th-century warship's anchor directly; the album is two centuries after her and the gap is stated. One more drawn witness in her own line since r206: the 문헌편's plates chapter (국립해양유산연구소, 학술총서 91집, pdf p. 143) reproduces the 귀선도 — two ink drawings of the roofed ship, 개인 소장 (최순선), on deposit with the 국가유산청 현충사관리소, undated in its caption — and both hang an anchor from the hull's end on a steeply angled shank with two curved arms crossing at the crown. In the two-masted drawing that end is unambiguously the BOW, beside the dragon head — the placement the drawn machine follows, against the encyclopedia's stern-drum variant named above; the roofed side view hangs the same form below its arched end-housing, and which end that housing caps is not resolved. The reproduction bounds the read: the ship spans about 1,500 px on the 300-dpi page — roughly 50 px/m if she is near the 도설's scale — and the anchor about 200 px, so the two-armed crossed form and the bow station are legible and nothing finer: no stone, no lashing, no stock can be affirmed or denied at that scale.
hull.windlassProvenance: The horong (호롱, 揚錨機), the Korean tradition's bow anchor-windlass — a NAVY-TRADITION EXTENSION, stated here, not a ship attestation: her own attestation is generated, and no fetched source puts a windlass on a 16th-century warship directly. The machine is attested three ways in her line. Her navy's own album, the Gakseondobon (c. 1797), carries it on the grain-ship plate: the National Maritime Heritage Institute's 2011 reconstruction of that plate (24 m) sets the horong at the bow, and the launch record says the horong was recreated from the drawing. The institute's component classification of the excavated Goryeo ships lists the horong among the anchoring gear (정박구: 닻, 호롱, 닻돌, 엄말) — read in the institute's site excerpts; the carrying page was not pinned, and no claim is made that a wreck preserved a horong timber. The living tradition gives the machine's working: a drum with two long bars passed through at different points, crossed, four men at the ends, about one coil of cable wound on (옛 돛단배의 언어 3). The album's warship plate draws the anchor; whether it also draws the windlass is NOT established by the sources fetched. CONTESTED placement: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture's hanseon description fixes an anchor-winding drum at the STERN board beside the rudder; the drawn machine follows the naval line's build record, at the bow. Station u 0.10 is a PHOTO/TEXT read, +/-0.05 (the open foredeck abaft the stem, forward of the sangjang's drawn leading edge at u 0.16; the launch photo resolves about 19 px/m — form only, no dimension can be read from it). Barrel 2.7 m is a GEOMETRIC class default: the drawn deck is 4.7 m wide at the drawn station, the probe's own measure re-run r208 — it was 3.8 across the 5.79 m foredeck the 9.4 m shell drew, and when the shell came in to the record's ~7.6 m the barrel followed its own warrant, the deck it stands on, at the same side margins. Diameter 0.5 m, the 0.30 m underside and the two standards are Falconer 1769 CLASS DEFAULTS cross-tradition, as the cog (r173) and the junk (r174); the 2.0 m bars are a CLASS DEFAULT (0.75 m of grip beyond the drum each side, resting near-horizontal as the replica photo shows them left). throughBars is the tradition's own form read, replacing Falconer's single-ended handspikes for this record alone.
hull.jeonseoProvenance: The 이충무공전서 권수 도설's 귀선지제 (1795), read whole at 300 dpi from the institute's own print — 국립해양유산연구소, 『거북선 학술 복원 보고서 문헌편』 (전통 선박 조선 기술 Ⅷ, 학술총서 91집; fetched whole r205 from the institute's report board, nttId 4452, 127,831,863 bytes byte-exact; the volume is a pure image scan, zero fonts, so every read is a plate read), pdf pp. 121–123, hanmun and translation both on the page. The spec, entire: 저판(본판) 10 planks, 64자 8치 long, 12자 head / 14자 5치 waist / 10자 6치 tail; 현판(삼판) 7 a side, 7자 5치 high, lowest 68자 to topmost 113자, all 4치 thick; 노판 (bow transom) 4 planks 4자 high, a 현자포 hole each side through the second; 축판 (stern transom) 7 planks 7자 5치 high, 14자 5치 over 10자 6치, the sixth plank pierced 1자 2치 for the rudder (속명 치); 신방 rails, 가룡 crossbeams yoked at the bow 'like an ox's chest', 방패 bulwark 4자 3치 rail to rail; 개판(귀배판) 11 planks a side meeting scale-fashion with a 1자 5치 spine gap to raise and strike the masts; turtle head 4자 3치 × 3자, burning sulphur and saltpetre for smoke; 10 oars and 22 gunports a side with 12 doors; under-deck 24 rooms — 2 iron stores, 3 magazines, 19 crew berths — and a cabin each side above for captain and officers. The 좌수영 variant is printed as differences: 尺度長廣 與統制營龜船略同 — 'length and breadth about the same' — a 鬼頭 carved under the turtle head, 龜紋 painted on the cover, two doors a side, per-side gunhole counts 2/1/10/6, and 8 oars a side. THREE BOUNDS, the record's own: the editor states no earlier source recorded dimensions; states the 1795 통제영 ship differs from 충무공's original by 치수의 가감 — the numbers are the late dockyard ship's, two centuries after Myeongnyang; and the 도설 compares turtle ship to turtle ship only — the panokseon is named nowhere in it, so these numbers reach this card only through the roofing argument the card's own text carries. The foot is CONTESTED in the scholarship — 영조척 ~31.2 cm against 주척 ~20.8 — and both conversions are printed in the row. The 도설 text names NO ground tackle — no 닻, no 호롱 — so the anchor and windlass warrants on this card stand on the album, the excavations and the living tradition, unchanged by this read. A SECOND MEASURED RECORD in the same line since r208: the card's 1882 row is read from the 『각사등록』 통제영계록, Gojong 19 (1882), the 광서 정월 15일 승정원 개탁 entry — 一戰船 本板 長九十尺·廣十八尺·元高十一尺·船頭廣十五尺·船尾廣十二尺, 上粧 長一百五尺·廣三十九尺; 龜船 本板 長六十七尺·廣十三尺·元高十三尺·船頭廣十尺·船尾廣八尺, 上粧 長八十八尺·廣三十三尺; the 右別船 between them at 본판 67척 3촌 — read whole at 300 dpi from the same 문헌편's pdf pp. 135–137, hanmun and the volume's own Korean translation both on the page and agreeing column for column, and cross-checked against Hong 2025's 표 3, which sets the 1882 일전선 beside the 각선도본 전선 within 촌s. The register names no foot; the card's row prints both conversions, the 1795 row's own contest. THE 본문편 READ, r209 — 국립해양유산연구소, 『거북선 학술 복원 보고서 본문편』 (전통 선박 조선 기술 Ⅷ, 학술총서 91집, 2026; attachment /2 of the same board post, nttId 4452, 784,858,884 bytes byte-exact, 404 pages, image-only, so every read is a plate read; landed r208): pp. 110–112, the 통제영 turtle ship's hull form and structure. The report builds that ship on the 판옥선-line warship's flat-bottom construction, gives the bottom a 밑들기 rise of about 1.2척 at the bow and 1.0척 at the stern with the mid-body flat, keeps the upper deck's sheer gentle for the guns and the oars, and draws the body plan (그림 67) with the 상장 33척 wide over an upper hull 27척 wide, 3척 a side; 표 6 fixes 상요광 27 as the upper deck plank's mid breadth, 선요고/현요고 9.0/7.5 and 전고 20.5척, and the 기본 설계도 (p. 128) prints its foot: 1척 = 31.22 cm, the 영조척. The report's own bounds, from its 일러두기 (p. 2): the 도설 is a compilation two centuries after the war; the design is a reference model that tests functional possibility, not the original; and every drawing is an inferred design, not a measured one. That is the warrant behind the card's Beam row sentence on the 3척 overhang — a class witness from the institute's design, not a measurement of any ship. pp. 41–42, the 이순신 종가 귀선도: two drawings in private hands on deposit at 현충사, undated, in the 도설's own manner and put at about 1800; the report reads them as the 도설's image carried on in family transmission, not independent evidence, and their inscription's dimensions (bottom 10파, breadth 5파, length 13파) as a later rough understanding. pp. 44–45, the turtle-ship painting first shown in New York in 2004 (176 × 240 cm on silk, private): its inscription quotes the 1823 해동역사 almost verbatim, its firearms are 19th-century types, and its paint shows reworking, so the report ranks it a later visual reconstruction behind the primary texts. It draws the hull body and the 상장 as visibly separate structures, and the report says that may be the painter's convention and not the ship. Neither painting changes a number on this card. THE 문헌편 CLOSED, r210: the volume's remaining panokseon-bearing documents read whole at 113 dpi (pdf 7–12 and 123–127). 태종실록 태종 13년 2월 5일 (1413): the king, passing the 임진도 ferry, watches a 귀선 and a 왜선 fight a mock action. 태종 15년 7월 16일 (1415): 탁신's sixth point on the defences, 龜船之法 衝突衆敵 而敵不能害, with the order to build it sturdier and more skilfully. 선조실록 선조 25년 6월 21일 (1592): the 옥포–사천–당포–한산–안골포 campaign, the turtle ship first sent in at 사천 on 5월 29일 to fire its 총통 and burn the enemy ship. 당포파왜병장, 이순신's 1592 report: 別制龜船 前設龍頭 口放大砲 背植鐵尖 內能窺外 外不能窺內, the one contemporary description of the ship, and at 당포 倭船大如板屋者九隻 — nine Japanese ships as large as a panokseon, one carrying a 층루 three to four 장 high, under which the turtle ship's dragon mouth fired 현자 shot upward. 견내량파왜병장 and 조진수륙전사장: the turtle ship charges first and the panokseon follow (龜船先突 板屋次進), and a fleet of some 250 ships proposed by province. 난중일기 1592.2.27, 3.27 and 4.12: the turtle ship's gun trials. None of these documents carries a dimension of either ship. The one comparative size in the primary record is the 당포 sentence, the Japanese great ship as large as a panokseon. The name 귀선 is two centuries older than the panokseon: the 1413 and 1415 ship is a different vessel of the same name, and the report prints it first. THE 본문편 VII READ, r210 (pp. 210–214 and 227–232 at 113 dpi; the body-plan labels of pp. 111 and 213 confirmed at 300 dpi): the report's second design, the 전라좌수영 turtle ship. 표 28 (p. 212) repeats the 통제영's hull figures exactly — 전장 113, 본판장 64.8, 본판요광 14.5, 상요광 27 — and lowers the hull sides (선요고/현요고 8.0/7.5, 선두고 and 선미고 8.5, against 9.0/7.5 and 9.5/9.0) under a taller whole (전고 22.5 against 20.5). Its body plan (그림 196, p. 213) labels 27.8척 (상장광) over 27척 (상요광), and 표 29 (p. 230) prints 상장 요광 27.8척, 두광 20.4, 미광 13.8, with 13 crossbeams, 8 oars a side worked from a lowered 포판, 10 개판 ports and 6 bow ports a side. The 통제영's own table, 표 7 (p. 135), prints 상장 요광 33.8척, 두광 26.4, 미광 20.5, 15 crossbeams, 10 oars, 22 방패 ports and 12 doors a side, 12 개판 ports — 0.8척 over its body plan's 33. The crossbeams of both designs run past the 상장 edge: 가목 34.3척 under a 33.8척 deck (표 8, p. 136) and 28.6척 under 27.8 (표 30, p. 231). So one report sets the 상장 overhang at 3 to 3.4척 a side for the 통제영 ship and 0.4척 a side for the 좌수영 ship, on identical hull figures. The 통제영's 33 has the 1882 register behind it; the 좌수영's 27.8 has no register, only the 도설's sentence that the 좌수영 ship's dimensions were nearly the 통제영's. The Beam row now states both. With this read the research residual on this card is closed.

vessels.text:
The standard warship of Japan from the Sengoku wars to the end of the Edo bakufu. The name means "barrier ship": the ships that enforced the toll barriers (seki) the lords of the Inland Sea — above all the Murakami houses — maintained across their straits, stopping, taxing and if need be taking every hull that passed. A navy's ships were counted by their oars: under forty a kobaya, a scout and messenger; forty to eighty a sekibune; above that, with beam to carry a castle, an atakebune. The sekibune is the cruiser of the three — a long, narrow hull on a single sharp stem, lightly framed, shallow, and by every account of the Imjin War faster through the water than anything Korea sent against her.

Her construction is the Japanese coastal tradition put to war. A wasen carries no keel: a heavy flat bottom plank, broad side strakes edge-fastened with iron staples and nails, crossbeams whose ends pierce the planking, a square stern with a great hanging median rudder that can be raised in shoal water, and the sharp raked stem — a single plank, the mizu-oshi — that parts the water. Over nearly the whole length of the hull the shipwrights laid the sō-yagura, a full fighting deck, and walled it with tate-ita, shield planks pierced by sama — loopholes for bows and arquebuses. The single mast is unstepped before action and laid down the yagura roof, and the ship fights under her forty sculling ro alone, one man standing at each.

Her doctrine was the opposite of the panokseon's, and the two argued it out across the Imjin War (1592–1598). A sekibune's light frame cannot bear the recoil of heavy cannon, so she carried almost none: her weapons were the arquebus through the loophole and the grappling iron over the rail, and her speed existed to close the range and put swordsmen on the enemy's deck. Against Chinese and Korean coasters, and in the fleet actions of the Inland Sea, it worked. Against a Joseon line that stood off behind high timber and fired cannon, it mostly did not. At Myeongnyang on 26 October 1597 the tidal race barred the deep atakebune, so the 133 warships that entered the strait were led by sekibune — and thirteen panokseon anchored across the narrows destroyed about thirty of them, killing the fleet's van commander Kurushima Michifusa, without losing a ship.

The type outlived the war by two and a half centuries, because the Tokugawa peace was built partly on its back. In 1609 the shogunate confiscated every atakebune in Japan and capped the daimyo at ships of 500 koku, which made the sekibune the largest warship a lord could own; the great houses built them to the limit, lacquered and gilded them into gozabune, and rowed their lords to Edo in them on the alternate-attendance processions. The shogun's own, the red-lacquered Tenchi-maru of 1630 — 500 koku, 76 oars — served for 230 years and was broken up only in the 1860s, when the navy that replaced her class ran on steam.

No Sengoku sekibune survives; the classification by oar count is recorded, and every dimension here is a reconstruction from it, labelled derived where it is inference.

tower.what: The commander's cabin standing on the yagura abaft the mast — a closed plank house under a ridged plank roof, which is the form the Busan scroll of 1593 draws on hull after hull of the anchored fleet. The ship is commanded from it; in the Edo peace it grew into the lacquered state cabin of the gozabune.

hull.towerProvenance: The WALLED form is attested: the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593 (Univ. of Tokyo), this card's own plate, draws the yakata as a closed plank house with a ridged roof on hull after hull — the open pavilion drawn before round 117 was the class default (the panokseon's janggundae), not this plate. The PLAN is derived: no Sengoku sekibune survives, so the 4.5 x 2.8 m footprint, the 2.0 m eaves and the roof pitch are read off the scroll's hulls at ship scale — good to the nearest half metre, no finer. The scroll also hangs cloth in the wall openings of several cabins; since round 139 one opening a side is drawn with the cloth hung in it. The OPENING's size and place are derived — no cabin interior is attested, and the scroll resolves the openings only to ship scale — the cloth itself is the scroll's.
hull.makuProvenance: The CLOTH is attested: the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593, this card's own plate, hangs a white band under a dark scalloped hem along the yagura band on hull after hull of the anchored fleet, and the atakebune amidships wears the same dress inverted — dark with white scallops — under sail. The scroll draws NO plank belt at this band, so gunDeck.walls (the panokseon's sangjang belt, round 118) is refuted for this class by its own plate. The DIMENSIONS are derived: the scroll stretches the upperworks, so the band's depth in metres cannot be read off it — the drawn cloth fills the band the model's own rail and deck bound, and the ~0.7 m scallop bay (makuBayM) is read off the scroll at its ~16 px/m (a ~25 m hull drawn ~400 px long), good to the nearest half metre, no finer. The BORDER's place and cut are the plate's own: on every hull that resolves it — the atakebune above all, the same dress at better scale — the scallops hang from the band's HEAD, tangent, cut from one strip, white cusps rising between them to the hanging line; until round 170 the drawn valance hung spaced discs off the band's FOOT, the record's own sentence inverted. The drawn valance is one strip a side, contiguous semicircles of half the recorded bay; its depth (a semicircle's, half the bay) is a class default — the scroll's stretch bars a finer read. Whether a sekibune cruised with the maku hung is not attested — the scroll's fleet is anchored, the atakebune wears hers under sail — and the ends of the band are left open: the plate shows the cloth only in broadside.
hull.samaProvenance: The SLOTS are attested for the class: Japanese accounts of the sekibune have the so-yagura walled with tate-ita shield planks pierced by sama, firing slots for bow and arquebus — the wall's purpose on a hull that mounts no broadside. The COUNT, SIZE and HEIGHT are derived: no Sengoku sekibune survives, and the Busan scroll (~16 px/m) resolves the yagura band but not individual slots, so 13 a side is set from the oar-station rhythm the length itself is derived from, and each slot is drawn 0.10 m wide by 0.36 m tall, centred 0.90 m over the fighting deck — the height a man standing on that deck fires from. Since round 140 the slots are OPENINGS cut through the drawn plank, with reveal faces the plank's own thickness deep and a dark board behind each so the slot reads into the deck's shadow; before that each was a dark plate laid on the wall's face.
hull.windlassProvenance: JUDGED SILENT, r176 — the windlass question for this hull, opened by the r172 residual, closes with nothing drawn, and this field says why. Her tradition's machine is the rokuro, and it is not a windlass: the surviving spindle and the Hokyu-maru model at the Minamichita wasen museum (photographs read this round, form only, no scale on the pages) show a vertical tapered spindle standing between a lower deck and an overhead beam, two long bars passed through it crosswise at different heights, the rope winding at its foot. Both fetched descriptions place and rig it the same way: two sets inside the aft yagura house, the line from the masthead semi block over the stern tobi-guruma block, winding yard, tender and anchor from within the ship (Minamichita wasen museum; Museum of Maritime Science monoshiri sheet 28). Every attestation is the Edo cargo tradition — the bezaisen, a type that postdates this drawn ship — and the museum's own sentence treats the machine's installation aboard as a development within that tradition. No fetched source puts a rokuro, or any winch, on a sekibune or any Sengoku warship; the Murakami Suigun Museum states the sekibune and kobaya barely appear in contemporary documents or drawings at all. Drawing one would stack three unsourced inferences: era (1597 against Edo attestations), class (cargo to war, with no textual bridge like the Tiangong Kaiwu's statement that the ocean transport's gear was all the same), and placement (the attested stand is inside an aft working house between floor and beam; this ship's aft house is the commander's yakata). The record stays silent and the builder draws nothing. That her hands hoisted by direct pull is itself an inference, marked as one on the card. Scope: this judgment is for the drawn 1597 instance; the class ran to 1868, an Edo sekibune shares the attested machine's own era, and a drawn Edo instance would reopen the question.
hull.anchorProvenance: The PRESENCE and the FORM are the plate's and the era's. The card's own plate — the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593, Univ. of Tokyo — draws the anchored fleet riding to twisted cables and, at the barrier line's upper and lower ends, the anchor itself at the cable's end: stockless, short-shanked, four strongly recurved claws (crops read r187; the lower one is clipped at the sheet edge). The era and class evidence agrees and points at her: on Ishii Kenji's evidence (1983, via Matsui Hironobu, Kanazawa Univ. archaeology bulletin 34, 2013, the four-claw iron anchor's typological study) — the anchor drawn in the 1433 Jingu Kogo engi emaki, and the 1486 Boshi nyuminki recording iron anchors on the Ming embassy ships — warships and special ships carried the four-claw iron anchor alongside wood-stone anchors from the first half of the 15th century, while wood and stone stayed the ordinary wasen's mainstay until the mid-17th: an early-1600s Osaka screen counts one iron anchor to eight wood-stone. The NAME and the making are the wasen tradition's: the Minamichita wasen museum's sentence — a square iron bar, its tip split in four and the quarters bent outward into claws, the count varying with the ship's size — and the Tomo anchor-smiths' recorded process (Tamura 1978, via Matsui). Every DIMENSION is a named default: no sekibune anchor survives. The drawn 2.0 m overall sits inside Matsui's measured corpus of 49 survivors (1.05–3.03 m, nearly all Edo–Meiji), at the corpus's own small/large break — about 120 kg by the Kozushima seabed anchor's calibration (2.8 m raised at 330–340 kg), a direct-pull load for a crew whose rokuro is judged silent (r176); ring and arm proportions follow the corpus and Matsui's fig. 1. The plate is at ship scale (~16 px/m) and no dimension is taken from it. COUNT is not recorded: one is drawn; Ishii's sentence has iron used alongside wood-stone on the warships, and that mixed tackle is not drawn — no count or mix is attested for her class. The STOW is a placement inference, the fleet rule (r182–r186): recovered on the open foredeck forward of the so-yagura — the bow is where the tradition works its anchor: the Edo bezaisen rests it on the uwakannuki, a hard-oak member on the bow's topmost rail, and belays the cable there (Minamichita, the same page; that beam is Edo cargo structure and is not drawn) — rolled 45 degrees, pitched to the deck's own gradient, settled by measured box; the cable bent to the free accessory ring and flaked in a coil beside it — no belay is attested and she has no winding machine. A measured Sengoku warship anchor, or the 1433 emaki plate in resolution, replaces the defaults and this field says so. Member sections are the corpus's own record, read r191: 表1 of the same paper (Matsui 2013 p.38) measures all 49 anchors at member level, and the arms are RECTANGULAR forged bars — 最大幅×最大厚 at the root, a wide thin blade at the fluke tip. Corpus means for the 27 consistently-printed anchors ≥190 cm, as fractions of 全長: root 0.0346±0.0037 × 0.0198±0.0033, tip 0.0220±0.0052 × 0.0058±0.0031. Both rings take the type anchor the class already cites (Onominato a: teardrop 44×19 cm of 3 cm bar, accessory ring ⌀36 of 4×4.5 section, on 269 cm). The weight field kg 122 is DERIVED by cube-law from the corpus's one weighed anchor — the Kozushima wreck anchor, 2.8 m, 330–340 kg by forklift (約90貫), raised 1990 — 15.26 kg per m³ of 全長³. The shank's two stations are the Pacific corpus's own calipers, read r192: 表3 of 二宮俊洋's master's survey (東京海洋大学 2014, oacis record 1018 — 144 anchors, Ibaraki to Wakayama, the companion survey to Matsui's) records the shank per anchor at the clean upper bar (軸正面×軸側面) and at the root boss where the four arms are forged on (軸根本正面×軸根本側面). Corpus means as fractions of 全長, each anchor's pair sorted (min,max) because the shrine's mounting sets which face is 正面: upper bar 0.0214±0.0046 × 0.0303±0.0058 (n=17), root boss 0.0491±0.0072 × 0.0764±0.0099 (n=16); excluded by name №1 (sea-concreted, every member ~2× corpus), №74 (exfoliated to 0.012 of 全長) and №93 (printed-inconsistent, a 0.36·全長 root), and №82's shaft pair flagged (側面/正面 = 2.8, twice anyone else) and dropped. The r191 CONTEST is RESOLVED, in the record's favour on both sides: the monument photographs' 0.023–0.034 was the upper bar, and the old solve's 0.047 was the root boss (0.0491) — the real shank tapers hard from an oblong boss to a slender near-square bar, and both prior readings were right at their own stations. The drawn shank now carries exactly those stations; the knee where the taper meets the bar is the one dimension no table records, SOLVED so the drawn iron weighs the record's kg at 7850 kg/m³ — at (2.0 m, 122 kg) it lands at 77% of the shank, inside the drawn form's own solvable band (69–138 kg); a record outside that band would clamp the knee and the mass audit would convict, a contest and not a knob. Cross-corpus check on the members already held: №71 (銚子, 300 cm) calipers claw root 0.0350×0.0233 and claw length 0.320 of 全長 against Matsui's 0.0346×0.0198 and the drawn 0.30 — two independent coasts agree on the arms. Residual: the mass calibration still hangs on the Kozushima weighing alone (約90貫 by forklift); the 1993 site report (東京都教育委員会, per the nabunken bibliography — print only, not surfaced open) would firm the kg, no longer the shank. The audit holds the drawn iron to the record's weight (V-YMASS, 12%) and the drawn shank's end sections to the calipered stations (V-YSHANK, 12%).

vessels.text:
A cargo vessel designed by shipwrights of Hoorn in the Dutch Republic in the 1590s and built to no other purpose. The hull is pear-shaped in section, broad in the hold and narrow at the deck, with a shallow draught that let it reach ports and rivers closed to deeper ships. Armament was minimised or omitted to leave the hold clear, which restricted it to waters where it did not expect to fight.

It was built of softwood cut by wind-powered sawmills and rigged so that twelve to fifteen men could work it where an English ship of the same burden needed about thirty. It carried roughly twice the cargo of its rivals at about half the freight cost.

⚠ The narrow deck is often explained as evasion of the Danish Sound Toll, which is said to have been charged on deck area. **The Sound Toll Registers do not support it**: officers assessed dues from the bills of lading a master presented, not from any measurement of the ship. The shape follows from what the hull is for — hold volume below, and as little weight and rigging as possible above.
vessels.cite: Unger, *Dutch Shipbuilding before 1800*; Sound Toll Registers Online; Wikipedia, *Fluyt* (accessed 2026-08-02).

vessels.text:
A three-masted armed merchantman chartered by the European East India companies for the Asia trade: the British EIC from 1600 to 1834, the Dutch VOC through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with French, Danish, Swedish, Austrian and Portuguese equivalents. British ships ran 1,100–1,400 tons burden. They carried substantial armament against pirates and privateers, which is why a merchant hull of the period is built to the proportions of a warship.

Solar and de Zwart worked the Dutch-Asiatic Shipping database, which records every VOC voyage made. **VOC ships were slow, and they did not get faster.** Mean passage to Batavia was 253 days in 1770–75 and 238 in 1783–92, and there is 'no significant trend' across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries at all.

English East Indiamen did the same passage in 173 days. The gap is 60–80 days between two fleets sailing the same ocean in the same years, and it is a fact about the hulls and the standing orders, not about the wind: Dutch hull form was constrained by shallow inland waterways, copper sheathing was adopted late, and the sailing instructions were conservative.

vessels.text:
Roughly half of all line-of-battle ships by 1800 were 74s: the point on the curve where enough guns met enough speed.

The manning ratio distinguishes a warship from any other vessel of the period. A merchantman carried one man per 20–30 tons; *Victory* carried one per 2.6. Guns need hands, and the Royal Navy went from 16,000 men in 1739 to 145,000 in 1813, roughly half the wartime lower deck pressed. Of about 103,000 deaths between 1793 and 1815, **81% were disease and accident, 13% shipwreck and fire, and 6% enemy action.**

rows: **454 people** permitted by the 1788 Act; reportedly as many as **609** carried before it
2.3 people per ton — the ratio the Act was written to reduce
vessels.text:
For three centuries the principal cargo carried across the Atlantic was people. An estimated 12.5 million were embarked and 10.7 million landed.

The between-decks of a slave ship was a designed space, drawn by naval architects and optimised for a quantity of human beings per ton, and the optimisation is legible in the numbers: mortality fell across three centuries not because conditions became humane but because passages got shorter and the loss of cargo was expensive.

The crew figure is the one that moved Parliament. Thomas Clarkson's evidence was drawn from muster rolls showing that about a fifth of the **crews** died too — a trade that killed the people who ran it at a rate comparable to the people it carried.

*The voyage database that records all of this is licensed for non-commercial use only, so this model cites it and does not republish it. The figures here are the published aggregates.*
vessels.cite: Eltis & Richardson, *Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade*; SlaveVoyages.org (cited, not redistributed — CC BY-NC).

The recorded 30 m (98 ft) is the ship's hull length (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_(1781_ship)), and the Brookes plan (Regulated Slave Trade Act plates, 1788–89) draws a raked stem carrying the head forward and a counter stern — the bow's share of the overhang larger than the stern's. vessels.name: Wyoming
vessels.sub: the longest wooden ship ever built
rows: 350 ft (106.7 m) on deck, 329.5 ft (100.4 m) between perpendiculars — beam 15.3 m, depth of hold 10 m
450 ft (137 m), jibboom tip to spanker boom tip
foundered off Cape Cod, 11 March 1924, all hands
vessels.text:
Wyoming was at or past the practical limit for a wooden hull: she worked in a seaway badly enough to need steam pumps continuously, and she was lost with all hands in 1924.

At 350 ft on deck — 106.7 m of wooden hull — she was too long to hold herself straight. A wooden hull resists bending only through the friction and fastenings between thousands of separate timbers, and past a certain length the sea simply works them: her planks twisted and opened, and **she ran her pumps continuously to stay afloat**. Not in heavy weather — always.

She foundered in a gale off Cape Cod in 1924 with everyone aboard. Iron and steel did not replace wood because they were cheaper; they replaced it because a metal hull is one continuous member and a wooden one is a negotiation.

And the rig is the other half of the story. Six masts of gaff sail are worked entirely from the deck — nobody goes aloft to reef — so she carried 3,730 tons with **thirteen people**. A square-rigged ship of that tonnage wanted thirty.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Wyoming (schooner)*, citing the Percy & Small yard records.

vessels.name: Preussen
vessels.sub: the largest sailing ship ever built
rows: 134.0 m hull (439.6 ft), 124 m waterline, 122 m between perpendiculars — beam 16.4 m
147 m (482 ft) over all, including the jibboom
five-masted full-rigger — the only one ever built
58 m deck to truck (68 m from the keel), one figure for all five — the standard rig cut interchangeable spars. Main course yard 32 m, royal 16 m.
426 nautical miles (1904); 20.5 kn at her fastest
vessels.text:
She was the largest sailing ship ever built and among the last commercially viable ones. She was lost in 1910 after a collision with a cross-Channel steamer that misjudged her speed.

Five masts, all square-rigged — the only ship ever built that way. 6,806 m² of canvas driving 5,081 tons round Cape Horn with nitrate, on a route where steam still could not compete because there was nowhere to coal.

In November 1910 the cross-Channel steamer *Brighton* misjudged her speed and tried to cross her bows. Preussen was making 16 knots. She broke her keel going ashore near Dover and was never salvaged.

That is the ending sail actually got: not obsolescence, but a steamer in a hurry.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Preussen (ship)*; Laeisz Flying-P line records.

polar.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

vessels.name: Great Eastern
rows: 211 m — beam 25.3 m, 18,915 gross register tons
six times the tonnage of any ship then afloat; unsurpassed for 40 years
17 m paddle wheels AND a 7.3 m screw AND six masts of sail
topsail schooner — a gaff sail on each of six masts
named for the days of the week: Monday forward to Saturday aft
steam to Australia and back without coaling
vessels.text:
Brunel built a ship six times bigger than anything afloat, and there was no trade for her.

The engineering was sound and the reasoning was sound: coal is the constraint on steam, and a bigger hull carries proportionally more of it, so a big enough ship could reach Australia without refuelling. She could. Nobody wanted to go to Australia in those numbers.

She spent her career unprofitable and ended doing the one job that needed a hull that size: **laying the Atlantic telegraph cable**, 4,200 km of it in one bottom. No other ship on earth could hold it.

No ship exceeded her tonnage for forty years.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *SS Great Eastern*; Brunel's own calculations on the coal fraction.

polar.rigNote: Paddle and screw together, six masts of sail above them as insurance. The wind decides little; coal and the size of her bunkers decide everything, which was the design argument.

The deck beneath is Brunel's double cellular iron top on the Britannia-bridge principle, two half-inch plates top and bottom on longitudinal webs (Descriptive Particulars of the Great Eastern Steam Ship, 1857) - so the teak is a covering laid over iron, which is what this model draws. No plank dimensions are attested; the drawn planks are class defaults.

vessels.name: Titanic
rows: 16, with 15 bulkheads — which stopped at D deck
21 kn service, 23 kn maximum — deliberately not a record-breaker
four, but only THREE drew smoke; the aftermost was a dummy
vessels.text:
She was not built to be fast. Cunard had the speed record and White Star chose not to compete for it — Titanic was built for **size and comfort**, on the theory that passengers would rather cross well than quickly.

Her sixteen watertight compartments were real, and they were not enough for a reason of geometry rather than engineering: **the bulkheads stopped at D deck**. Water filling one compartment past that level simply flowed over the top into the next. She could float with four flooded. The iceberg opened five.

The lifeboat number was legal. The regulation scaled boats to a ship's TONNAGE and had last been written when the largest ship afloat was 10,000 tons.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *RMS Titanic*; British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry, 1912.

polar.rigNote: Does not care about the wind. Its constraint is coal: the bunker fraction, not the weather, decides where it can go.

anchor.source: British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry; Olympic-class service records: 21–22 kn at sea

Planks 5 in wide by 3 in thick - 127 x 76 mm. The pitch-pine ends and the teak margins are finer distinctions than this one-covering model draws.

vessels.name: Unmanned surface vessel
vessels.sub: nobody aboard — a rigid wing, and no canvas
rows: wind, wave and solar; diesel-electric on some hulls
months, limited by fouling and machinery, not by stores
fastest uncrewed Atlantic crossing, Bermuda to the UK, August 2019
first fully autonomous sea voyage — 240 km in 7 hours, 17 Jan 2022
first autonomous cargo ship, launched Nov 2021; all-electric
German remote-controlled FL-boats in the First World War; US Navy target and minesweeping craft in the Second
survey, hydrography, ocean monitoring, naval picket
3–5 kn under wind and solar — **contested** as a 'service' figure for a hull that harvests its own drive; burst speeds are higher on diesel-electric types
vessels.text:
A vessel that operates on the surface without a crew aboard, across a range from remote control to full autonomy. Propulsion may be wind, wave or solar: a wave glider takes its drive from the motion of the sea itself, and a Saildrone from wind and sunlight.

Removing the crew changes the constraint. A crewed ship's endurance is set by food, water and human tolerance; take the crew off and the limits become fouling, machinery and power. A wind-and-solar hull can stay out for **months**, and the sea state that would be dangerous for a manned vessel is merely slow for one that cannot drown.

It is a strange place for this story to arrive. The whole history above is people solving the problem of getting themselves across an ocean — and the current answer, for a growing share of the work, is not to go.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Unmanned surface vehicle*; Saildrone and NOAA survey programmes.

polar.rigNote: Harvests its drive from wind, wave and sun — slow everywhere rather than fast somewhere. The design axis is endurance: months at sea, no one to feed.

anchor.source: Saildrone / wave-glider published figures: 3–5 kn under wind and solar
anchor.note: contested as a service figure — her own card row says so

hull.rakeProvenance: Generated type record: the card's '~22 m' and the lwl 20.5 are composite figures for the survey-USV class (Saildrone's current sheet gives Surveyor 20 m; earlier Surveyor material said 72 ft). The 1.5 m allowance is filled at the authored 3:1 bow:stern character of the type's raked-stem hulls - authored and qualitative, not attested to the centimetre; drawn planking spans 22.00 exactly.

vessels.name: Clipper
rows: ⚠ **not a sailplan.** A clipper is a hull — fine lines built for speed. Clippers were schooners, brigs and brigantines as well as full-rigged ships
hull 64.8 m, beam 10.97 m, 963 gross register tons
363 nm — a 15.1 kn average sustained for 24 hours
*Champion of the Seas*, 465 nm in 1854 — unbeaten until 1984
composite after 1863 — iron framework, wooden planking
boom from 1843; ended by the Panama Railroad (1855) and Suez (1869)
vessels.text:
The fastest commercial sailing ships ever built, and they were obsolete almost immediately.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869, the year *Cutty Sark* was launched. It cut London–Bombay from about 10,600 nautical miles to 6,200 — and **sail could not use it**, because there is no wind in a cut and towage was charged. So the clippers were driven onto the routes the canal did not help: Australian wool, and Chilean nitrate round the Horn. They were the best answer to a question that had just stopped being asked.

The rival record is worth the argument it causes. *Andrew Jackson*'s 89 days 4 hours in 1860 was measured pilot-to-pilot at the Farallones, after which she lay all night waiting for a pilot; Cutler put her anchor-to-anchor time at possibly 89 days 20 hours. The two figures are not commensurable.
vessels.cite: Cutler, *Greyhounds of the Sea*; Royal Museums Greenwich.

polar.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

anchor.source: Lubbock, The Log of the Cutty Sark: 17.5 kn logged; 363 nm/24 h sustained

hull.capstanProvenance: Bar capstan of the European tradition, a type-period CLASS DEFAULT — no hull-specific plate; counts are class defaults (whelps 6: Falconer 1769 pl. II figs 11-12 resolve six, period range 6-8). Form and proportions from Falconer 1769 CAPSTERN (whelps drumhead-to-deck like buttresses, chocks, two iron pawls, bars heaved at the breast) and pl. II fig 11 (engraving, widths ~±10%: height ≈ 0.86 of drumhead dia, neck sweep 0.82 flaring to 1.0 at the deck). Sized to the men at its bars.

vessels.name: Ocean steamer
rows: paddle wheels — impractical in a seaway and abandoned for the screw; turbines from *Lusitania* and *Mauretania*; diesel and oil firing from the early 1930s
under 10 kn — twelve days and more
34.5 kn — 3 days 12 hours, and the record still stands
vessels.text:
An iron-hulled, screw-driven steamship on a scheduled ocean route. The figure that governs its range is not horsepower but **pounds of coal per horsepower-hour**, which fell about threefold between 1855 and 1890.

That is what made steam viable on long routes. At 1850s efficiency a ship crossing an ocean had to give up roughly half its deadweight to its own fuel; by 1890 it was 15–20%. Nothing about the engine's power mattered as much as how little coal it burned to make it.

Compound expansion (1854), triple expansion (A. C. Kirk, 1881), then the turbine and oil firing. Steam overtook sail on the British register around 1883.
vessels.cite: Griffiths, *Steam at Sea*; Kirk on triple expansion, 1881.

polar.rigNote: Does not care about the wind. Its constraint is coal: the bunker fraction, not the weather, decides where it can go.

anchor.source: her own rows: Atlantic passages of the early screw era under 10 kn; trial 12.25 stands as speedKn

vessels.name: HMS Dreadnought
vessels.sub: the ship that made every other obsolete
rows: 21 kn — turbines, the first capital ship to have them
ten 12-inch guns in five twin turrets
one year and one day, Portsmouth, 1905–06
steel-wire torpedo nets on 40 ft booms; landed early in WWI
vessels.text:
A battleship carrying a uniform main battery of ten 12-inch guns and driven by steam turbines, completed at Portsmouth in a year and a day. Both features were already understood separately; putting them in one hull made every existing battleship in every navy second-rate at a stroke, and the type took her name.

The all-big-gun battery follows from gunnery rather than from ambition. Fire control works by observing the fall of shot and correcting, and that is only possible if every splash comes from a gun of the same calibre — a mixed battery gives you two sets of splashes and no way to tell which is which at the ranges the guns could already reach.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *HMS Dreadnought (1906)*; Wikipedia, *Gerald R. Ford-class* (accessed 2026-08-03).

vessels.name: Yamato
vessels.sub: 大和 — the largest guns ever put to sea
rows: nine 46 cm (18.1 in) guns — three triple turrets
belt 410 mm · deck 200–226 mm · turret face **650 mm**
twelve 12.7 cm in six twin mounts; twenty-four 25 mm in eight triple mounts — by 1945 the 25 mm barrels numbered about 150
up to seven floatplanes; two stern catapults and a crane. Boats and aircraft stowed BELOW decks — 46 cm muzzle blast would wreck anything left in the open
vessels.text:
The heaviest battleship ever built, carrying the largest naval guns ever mounted: nine 46 cm rifles in three triple turrets, behind a belt of 410 mm and a turret face of 650 mm.

She was sunk on 7 April 1945 by carrier aircraft, having barely fired those guns at an enemy ship. The armour was proof against the shells it was designed against, and the attack came from above.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Japanese battleship Yamato* (accessed 2026-08-03).

Neighbouring cypresses of the same pale colour class, so the drawn tone stands either way. Plank width 127 mm from Skulski; butt length is a class default.

vessels.name: Supercarrier
vessels.sub: Gerald R. Ford class · the deck is the weapon
rows: 41 m at the waterline — but **78 m across the flight deck**
two A1B reactors, four shafts, in excess of 30 kn
vessels.text:
A nuclear-powered aircraft carrier of about 100,000 tons. Its waterline beam is 41 m and its flight deck is 78 m across, because the deck overhangs the hull on both sides — the two numbers describe different things and neither alone describes the ship.

The angled deck is the feature everything else depends on. A landing strip set a few degrees to port means a pilot who misses the arrestor wires flies off the bow and goes round again, instead of into the aircraft parked forward behind a crash barrier. The island is small and to starboard so the deck stays clear, and to starboard specifically because an aircraft going around swings to port.

Two reactors remove the constraint that shaped every warship before: a hull that no longer carries its own fuel can spend that volume and that range on aircraft instead.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier* (accessed 2026-08-03).

polar.rigNote: Weather is a delay, not a route.

anchor.source: US Navy published figure for the class: "30+ knots"

Ford - and it is not a shell length: the flight deck is its own attested plate at 1,092 x 256 ft (333 x 78 m), and no source publishes the shell's length between extremities. The rakes 0.03/0.02 are reconstruction; the drawn planking spans 333.85, INSIDE the record's loa. The deck is drawn at flightDeckLen 333.0, anchored so the aft round-down overhangs the fantail and the span from the shell's bow tip to the round-down is 337.00 = loa exactly. A planking-only sweep reads -3.15 on this hull by construction; that is the record's geometry, not an under-fill.

vessels.name: Container ship
rows: 21 container slots — the first container ship, a quarter-century before the intermodal box
40-foot units are about 90% of all container shipping
~90% of non-bulk cargo; over 80% of world freight by volume
16–25 kn; slow steaming cut this to about 21 kn in the 2010s

**derived** — 33.2 m depth moulded (MSC Gülsün class, *Significant Ships of 2019*) less the 16 m loaded draught = 17.2 m to the weather deck; this is a type ship, a composite of the class, not one hull
LOA 294.13 m, beam 32.31 m, draught 12.04 m
LOA 366 m, draught 15.2 m; beam **contested** — 49 m as built, raised to 51.25 m by the Canal Authority in 2018

vessels.text:
The last chapter of this story is not about the sea at all. A modern container ship's route is set by **lock chambers and dredged channels** — numbers written down by engineers — rather than by anything the ocean does.

Panamax is not a ship. It is the inside dimension of a lock built in 1914, and for a century the world's fleet was designed around it: 294.13 m long, 32.31 m in the beam, because that is what fits. The 2016 expansion moved the number and the fleet moved with it.

Growth has now stopped, and it stopped on port depth and canal width rather than on anything to do with naval architecture.
vessels.cite: Levinson, *The Box* (2006); Panama Canal Authority vessel requirements; Suez Canal Authority.

The old 30.0 had no source and stood the deck at nearly the whole moulded depth over the water — a hull floating near her light line drawn as loaded. The statutory summer freeboard is smaller still and is measured to a lower freeboard deck, not the weather deck this model lofts — the same distinction ever-given's stationProvenance records from her casualty report.

20,124 TEU on 399.94 m — among the largest afloat
23 March 2021, Suez Canal km 151, at 13 knots in a sandstorm
369 ships waiting; roughly 12% of world trade passes the canal
vessels.text:
Ever Given is a 20,124 TEU container ship built by Imabari Shipbuilding in 2018 and operated by Evergreen Marine. At 399.94 m she is a metre short of the 400 m at which some port and canal rules change, which is not a coincidence: the largest ships are built to the dimensions of the infrastructure that must accept them.

On the morning of 23 March 2021 she entered the Suez Canal southbound at about 13 knots in a sandstorm with gusts above 40 knots, sheered, and grounded diagonally across the channel at kilometre 151, wedging her bulbous bow into the eastern bank. The canal is single-lane along that stretch and there is no way past. She was refloated on 29 March after 163 hours, by dredging roughly 30,000 cubic metres from around the bow, fourteen tugs, and a spring tide.

By the time she moved, 369 ships were waiting at both ends. Around 12 per cent of world trade passes through the canal, and the alternative — round the Cape — adds about 9,000 km and ten days. The blockage is the clearest demonstration this model has of its own last chapter's argument: a modern route is set by the dimensions of dredged channels and lock chambers, and one hull athwart one of them stops a system that has no slack in it.
vessels.cite: Suez Canal Authority; Marine Accident Investigation Branch interim report, 2021.

180.6 m — longer than any private vessel then afloat
4.3 m, unusually shallow for the length, for Gulf and Red Sea waters
two gas turbines and two diesels, about 94,000 shaft horsepower
above 30 knots — faster than most warships of her displacement

vessels.text:
Azzam was delivered by Lürssen in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan and at 180.6 m remains the longest private motor yacht built. She is included here as the end point of a line the rest of this model traces: for most of history the largest and most advanced hulls afloat were built to carry cargo, fight, or explore, and their size was justified by what they returned.

Her engineering is not decorative. A combined diesel and gas turbine plant of roughly 94,000 shaft horsepower drives four waterjets to over 30 knots — faster than most warships of comparable displacement — and she draws only 4.3 m on that length, a deliberately shallow hull for Gulf and Red Sea waters that forced a very fine, wide, low-block form.

The type is a real category rather than a curiosity: yachts above 100 m are now built in numbers, and they sustain specialist yards, naval-architecture practices and a supply chain that overlaps with naval work.
vessels.cite: Lürssen; Boat International Global Order Book.

vessels.name: Endurance
vessels.sub: crushed in the Weddell Sea, found in 2022

polar.rig: barquentine — square on the fore, fore-and-aft on main and mizzen
polar.rigNote: Square canvas on the foremast only, with fore-and-aft main and mizzen, plus a 350 ihp coal-fired auxiliary. The rig is a compromise for ice work: enough square sail to run before the westerlies, few enough yards that a small crew can handle her among floes, and an engine for calms and leads.

anchor.source: Framnæs builder's figure under steam, 1912; under sail alone she was slower

floor.source: auxiliary steam floor; no measured headwind figure survives, so the loss follows the clipper's fractional windage — an inference

hull.stationProvenance: Masts, funnel, deckhouses and overhangs READ off the Framnaes longitudinal-section plan (as Polaris, RMG J9266, web copy 1024x322 px, ~16.9 px/m along the hull — stations good to ±0.5 m, no finer), anchored at the stem and counter LWL crossings; mast-gap ratio and funnel station cross-checked against the Hurley broadside (RMG P00018, ~12.6 px/m: fore-main/main-mizzen 1.12, funnel 45% of main→mizzen). Trucks from the same broadside at 12.6 px/m: fore 34.3 m, main 35.2 m, mizzen 29.3 m over the water, main the tallest — the old record drew the fore at 49 m (27.5 m lower through the square-stack rule) and the main at 31.7. Funnel at 0.677: the plan reads 0.670 +/- 0.015 and the boiler casing must seat inside the house whose forward end it rises from. Funnel black: it reads as dark as the black hull in every plate where masts read pale; height 5.7 m over the rail at the broadside’s scale. No forward deckhouse: the plan shows a boat on skids between fore and main, and no photograph shows a house there. Quarter boats (davitBoats): a canvas-covered boat hangs outboard in radial davits on the port quarter in the Hurley night plate and two stand on the starboard side in the full-sail plate; both plates are bow-on and foreshortened, so the station is bounded, not measured — abaft the aft house (plan, 0.781) and clear of the counter, u 0.80 ± 0.04. Length 6.7 m: the expedition's cutters (Dudley Docker, Stancomb Wills) as recorded; the James Caird measured 6.9. Kept: the forecastle break — the web plan at 16.9 px/m cannot carry a clean break station or height (the deck lines there are one to two px apart); needs the RMG original before it is modelled.
hull.capstanProvenance: Bar capstan of the European tradition, a type-period CLASS DEFAULT — no hull-specific plate; counts are class defaults (whelps 6: Falconer 1769 pl. II figs 11-12 resolve six, period range 6-8). Form and proportions from Falconer 1769 CAPSTERN (whelps drumhead-to-deck like buttresses, chocks, two iron pawls, bars heaved at the breast) and pl. II fig 11 (engraving, widths ~±10%: height ≈ 0.86 of drumhead dia, neck sweep 0.82 flaring to 1.0 at the deck). Sized to the men at its bars.

rows: Framnæs, Sandefjord, 1912, as *Polaris* — for Arctic tourist cruising
oak and Norwegian fir, greenheart sheathing; stem 1.3 m thick
19 January 1915; drifted with the pack for ten months
5 March 2022, 3,008 m down, four miles from Worsley's fix
vessels.text:
Endurance was built at Framnæs in Sandefjord in 1912 as *Polaris*, for Arctic tourist cruising, and was designed for ice rather than merely strengthened against it: oak and Norwegian fir with greenheart sheathing, and a stem formed from a single baulk about 1.3 m thick. Shackleton bought her for the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition of 1914.

She was beset in the Weddell Sea pack on 19 January 1915, one day's sail from her intended landing, and drifted with the ice for ten months. A ship built for ice can survive pressure from the sides; what destroyed her was being lifted and racked as floes converged. She was abandoned on 27 October and sank on 21 November 1915. All twenty-eight men survived, by boat to Elephant Island and then by an 800-nautical-mile passage in the 6.9 m *James Caird* to South Georgia.

The wreck was located on 5 March 2022 at 3,008 m, about four nautical miles from the position Frank Worsley recorded by sextant as she went down — a navigational fix taken from an ice floe with no land in sight, and vindicated after a century.
vessels.cite: Endurance22 expedition; Worsley's navigational log; Alexander, *The Endurance* (1998).

vessels.name: Queen Mary 2
vessels.sub: the last ship built to cross, not to cruise

polar.rig: diesel-electric and gas turbine, four azimuthing pods
polar.rigNote: Four azimuthing pods, two fixed and two steerable, fed by diesel-electric plant with gas turbines for the top end — about 117 MW. Pods rather than shafts because a liner hull fine enough to hold 26 knots in a North Atlantic winter has no room for four shaft lines.

anchor.source: Chantiers de l'Atlantique sea trials, 2003

tierBands.provenance: DERIVED from a broadside photograph (Paul Coueslant, Southampton Water, geograph.org.uk 5649661, CC BY-SA 2.0, 2018): every tier above the boat gallery is a balcony row, a dark void over roughly two-thirds of the tier height divided at cabin pitch of about 2.6 m.

hull.houseProvenance: DERIVED from the same photograph: the black tops out at the recorded 17 m sheer; above it the shell plating carries up two further decks in a WHITE sheer strake with a continuous square-window row on each (shellTiers 2, painted shellTopside), so the boat gallery floor lands at 17 + 2·3.2 = 23.4 m over water — the photograph reads it at about 24 m with the deck module as the scale. The black hull below the strake carries only sparse broken window groups and is drawn plain.

shellBands.provenance: DERIVED from the same broadside photograph: the white strake windows are about 1.4 m square at roughly 2.5 m pitch, a bold colonnade, not the 0.7 m C-deck lights the Edwardian default draws.

hull.housePlateProvenance: MEASURED off the scale profile (Wikimedia Commons, File:En mary titanic.svg, Yzmo, CC BY-SA 3.0) by segmenting her silhouette and reading, at every metre of height above the load waterline, the most-forward and most-aft column still standing at that height. houseAt fore end, houseCrest, tierForeU, tierAftU 7-8, the funnel station and its 24.3 m fore-and-aft length, and the mast at u 0.19 are all that measurement. Three earlier attempts were judged by eye off a 34-degree lens that magnifies the near half of a 345 m ship by a third. r162: tierAftU 2-6 re-measured off the aft-quarter photographs; see tierAftUProvenance. r163: tierAftU 1 and the houseAt aft end re-measured to the counter (the fantail edge, u 1.008); see tierAftUProvenance.
hull.topWorksProvenance: MEASURED from the same scale profile as houseAt/houseCrest (Commons, File:En mary titanic.svg, Yzmo, CC BY-SA 3.0): the runs of her silhouette standing above the 46.5 m top-deck line, each with its u-span and its peak height over the water. Heights here are above the crest roof.

deck.provenance: RECORDED for the promenade, EXTENDED above: Cunard's own copy and the Cunard historian Chris Frame carry the wrap-around Promenade Deck, deck 7, as laid teak, nearly 600 m to the lap - and deck 7 is this hull's sheer, so the model's weather deck IS the attested surface. The house tier decks above draw the same covering; photographs of her terraced stern show laid decking there, but no builder's figure attests it. The working foredeck's painted steel is a distinction this one-covering model does not draw. Replaces the deckSteel guess.
deck.roofsProvenance: TERRACES, NOT THE CREST: two plates at the era's two ends read laid decking on every aft terrace — the fantail and its pool, the cafe step, the main-pool terrace, the two shallow steps above — and white coated plate on the topmost roof where the dome and mast stand and on the large shell roof forward of the cascade. Plates: Commons 20161001 Queen Mary Aerial 2 (CC BY-SA 4.0, 3888 px, ~3.4 px/m at the stern) and the 2004-07-20 Hamburg arrival set (Arnold Schott, CC BY-SA 3.0, 1200 px, ~1.5 px/m) — colour-field reads, the fields metres wide, so both plates support them; scales and crops in Research/QM2-PLATES.md. Replaces the r108 'false', whose own sentence 'pale coated plate in every photograph' these photographs refute. The forward working deck's painted steel is still not drawn by this one-covering model.

hull.rakeProvenance: MEASURED off a bow plate — Wikimedia Commons File:Queen Mary 2 bow.jpg (Conollyb, CC BY 2.5, Sydney) — scaled by her name letters on the flare at about 1.5 m. Her stem overhangs the forward perpendicular by about 23.5 m; the model had 13.67 m, which is why she read blunt from ahead however fine the waterline under her. LOA 345 is fixed and already drawn exactly, so the overhang comes out of the perpendiculars: lwl is the length between them (318.2 m) and the transom keeps its 3.3 m counter — the same lwl-is-LBP semantics r131 established on the container ship and the slave ship. Every u-keyed feature is re-derived through the new frame from its own original plate reading, not rescaled from the old u.
hull.tierAftUProvenance: TIERS 2-6 MEASURED off the aft-quarter plates (Research/QM2-PLATES.md), replacing the r97 scale-drawing spans the r132 residual convicted: the drawing dealt seven near-equal steps with the deepest near the top, the photographs read five terraces with the deep ones low and mid. Method: each terrace depth counted in 2.6 m tierBands balcony bays on the 2016-10-01 aerial (CC BY-SA 4.0, 3888 px; every gap measured between deck edges at the SAME height so the one-story parallax cancels), chained downward from the kept crest foot t7 0.816: fantail 6 bays, cafe step 3, main-pool terrace 8, awning step 1, inter-row strip half, top step 5 bays AS BUILT - the record year is 2003 and the 2004-07-20 Hamburg pair reads the open top step about a bay deeper than the 2016 frame, whose refit cabin front took that bay (only the top step changed in the 2016 remastering). Integer bay counts, error a half-bay per edge (1.3 m, u 0.004). Chain closure: the predicted fantail edge lands at u 1.008 against the drawn counter extremity u 1.010. Crest block t7-t9 kept from the r97 profile (not this residual). r163: t1 and houseAt[1] moved to the chain-predicted fantail edge u 1.008 - the 2011 Southampton astern plate reads one continuous rounded shell from counter to fantail rail, and the strake face 0.992 was the scale drawing's stern column (the same weak link as tiers 2-6); the loft rides the counter for any pin past u 1.0. r164: the black paint rise is recorded (sternLivery) and drawn. r165: the balcony wings are recorded (tierWings) and drawn. r166: read 3b measured and closed - tier 7's aft rail curves (tierRound, 2.9 m sagitta), tiers 2/3 measure straight, 4-6 unresolved at plate resolution, and the fantail windscreen is recorded (fantailScreen).

sternLivery.provenance: MEASURED off the aft-quarter plates (Research/QM2-PLATES.md). At the stern face the hull black rises over the counter to the foot of the oval-row strake: plate 3 (2011 Southampton astern, 3296 px) reads ONE deck of white below the fantail rail, the name painted on black, and plates 1 (2016 aerial) and 2 (2004 Hamburg, as built) read the same at both ends of the era - so the black swallows the lowest 1 of the 2 white shell strakes (strakes), good to a quarter deck. fromU 0.93 is the knee where the line leaves the level 17 m sheer: ~29 m forward of the drawn tip on the 2016 aerial (the fantail's own 15.6 m span scales the quarter at ~18.5 px/m along-axis), a couple of bays forward of the fantail front 0.959, supported to +/- 2 bays (u +/- 0.016). The line is drawn straight in u from the sheer at fromU to the strake boundary at the stern extremity - the plates cannot adjudicate its exact curve - and the risen black is drawn unpierced: the plates show only sparse small lights in it.

tierWings.provenance: MEASURED off the 2016-10-01 aerial (Research/QM2-PLATES.md plate 1, read 3a; instrument build/staging/r165/measure-wings.py): the side balcony wings run aft past each terrace floor, so the terrace sits recessed between them. Wing tips in 2.6 m balcony bays aft of each tier's own recorded face, converted at 2.6/318.2 per bay: tier 4/5, the two-story cabin block on the main-pool terrace, 2.7 bays aft of the tier-5 face (port read, the starboard block corroborates), one tip for both stories, u 0.883; tier 7, the wing decks flanking the top terrace, 3 bays (port and starboard reads disagree 2-5, split and capped by the tier-6 roof they stand on), u 0.840; tier 2, the glazed gallery flanking the fantail, 1.5 bays aft of the pavilion face to its stair, u 0.971. Every read +/-1 bay (u 0.008), tier 7 +/-2. depthM is the wing's inboard extent from the deck edge: the block reads ~6 m (one outboard cabin and balcony, +/-2 m), the fantail gallery ~2.8 m, the tier-7 wing decks ~3 m. The longer lattice-railed runs aft of the block are deck-level balustrades, not enclosed wings, and are not recorded. Wing tips are drawn with a one-bay chamfer at the inboard corner, the angled ends both plates show; the plates cannot adjudicate the exact cut, and the chamfer length is a drawing choice at plate resolution.

tierRound.provenance: MEASURED off the 2016-10-01 aerial (Research/QM2-PLATES.md plate 1, read 3b; instrument build/staging/r166/measure-round.py, overlay z-t7-marked.png): the jacuzzi step's aft rail at tier 7 sweeps convex-aft between the r165 wing decks - apex 25 px aft of the chord through the notch corners at ~8.4 px/m along-axis, 2.9 m, +/-1.0 m (apex candidates spread 2.8-3.0 m; the image apex lands 60% along the chord, which is where an arc symmetric about the centreline lands seen obliquely). vessels.text:
Queen Mary 2 entered service in 2004 and is the only ocean liner still in scheduled service. The distinction from a cruise ship is structural rather than commercial. A liner is built to hold a schedule across the North Atlantic in winter, which requires speed in a seaway and a hull that can take it: she has a long, fine, flared bow with a real forecastle, shell plating up to about twice the thickness of a comparable cruise ship's, and a service speed of 26 knots against the 22 a cruise ship makes.

Her propulsion is four azimuthing pods, two fixed and two steerable, fed by diesel-electric and gas-turbine plant — an arrangement that gives her the power for the crossing without the shaft lines a hull of that fineness has no room for.

She is the last of the type. The transatlantic liner was killed by the jet within a decade of 1958, and everything built since for that water has been built to cruise. That one ship is still constructed to cross it is why she belongs at the end of this fleet.

crabclaw.rigNote: Poor by modern standards, positive by ancient ones — and positive is the whole argument, because it is what lets a canoe beat back the way she came. Fastest on a broad reach, not before the wind.
crabclaw.rig: crab claw on a double hull

square.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

lateen.rigNote: Better than a square rig, and by less than the textbooks claim — their 55–65° is a heading. The cost is manpower: tacking means walking the whole yard round the mast.

gaff.rigNote: Points high and is worked entirely from the deck — nobody goes aloft to reef a gaff sail. That is the whole economic argument for the rig: the crew, not the speed.

junk.rigNote: The battens do it: they make the sail self-reefing and let it set flat, so it beats a square rig to windward on a fraction of the crew — about 75–80% of Bermudan performance.

oar.rigNote: A galley goes where it likes and not far, and the figure above is her SAILING speed — the sail is for fair winds only. Under oar: 8.3 kn sprint, 5.4 kn cruise, and about 2.9 kn into a headwind with a metre of sea — measured on the reconstruction Olympias, which fell short of what the ancient sources imply and is thought to be ~10% too short in the hull.
oar.rig: oars, with a square sail for fair winds

steam.rigNote: Does not care about the wind. Its constraint is coal: the bunker fraction, not the weather, decides where it can go.
